2328        description: r##"# `abi_avr_interrupt`
2329
2330Allows `extern "avr-interrupt" fn()` and `extern "avr-non-blocking-interrupt" fn()`.
2331
2332The tracking issue for this feature is: [#69664]
2333
2334[#69664]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/69664

2339        warn_since: None,
2340        deny_since: None,

2342    Lint {
2343        label: "abi_cmse_nonsecure_call",
2344        description: r##"# `abi_cmse_nonsecure_call`
2345
2346The tracking issue for this feature is: [#81391]
2347
2348[#81391]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/81391
2349
2350------------------------
2351
2352The [TrustZone-M
2353feature](https://developer.arm.com/documentation/100690/latest/) is available
2354for targets with the Armv8-M architecture profile (`thumbv8m` in their target
2355name).
2356LLVM, the Rust compiler and the linker are providing
2357[support](https://developer.arm.com/documentation/ecm0359818/latest/) for the
2358TrustZone-M feature.
2359
2360One of the things provided with this unstable feature is the "cmse-nonsecure-call" function ABI.
2361This ABI is used on function pointers to non-secure code to mark a non-secure function call
2362(see [section 5.5](https://developer.arm.com/documentation/ecm0359818/latest/) for details).
2363
2364With this ABI, the compiler will do the following to perform the call:
2365* save registers needed after the call to Secure memory
2366* clear all registers that might contain confidential information
2367* clear the Least Significant Bit of the function address
2368* branches using the BLXNS instruction
2369
2370To avoid using the non-secure stack, the compiler will constrain the number and
2371type of parameters/return value.
2372
2373<!-- NOTE(ignore) this example is specific to thumbv8m targets -->
2374
2375``` rust,ignore
2376#![no_std]
2377#![feature(abi_cmse_nonsecure_call)]
2378
2379#[no_mangle]
2380pub fn call_nonsecure_function(addr: usize) -> u32 {
2381    let non_secure_function =
2382        unsafe { core::mem::transmute::<usize, extern "cmse-nonsecure-call" fn() -> u32>(addr) };
2383    non_secure_function()
2384}
2385```
2386
2387``` text
2388$ rustc --emit asm --crate-type lib --target thumbv8m.main-none-eabi function.rs
2389
2390call_nonsecure_function:
2391        .fnstart
2392        .save   {r7, lr}
2393        push    {r7, lr}
2394        .setfp  r7, sp
2395        mov     r7, sp
2396        .pad    #16
2397        sub     sp, #16
2398        str     r0, [sp, #12]
2399        ldr     r0, [sp, #12]
2400        str     r0, [sp, #8]
2401        b       .LBB0_1

2458
2459In the MSP430 architecture, interrupt handlers have a special calling
2460convention. You can use the `"msp430-interrupt"` ABI to make the compiler apply
2461the right calling convention to the interrupt handlers you define.
2462
2463<!-- NOTE(ignore) this example is specific to the msp430 target -->
2464
2465``` rust,ignore
2466#![feature(abi_msp430_interrupt)]
2467#![no_std]
2468
2469// Place the interrupt handler at the appropriate memory address
2470// (Alternatively, you can use `#[used]` and remove `pub` and `#[no_mangle]`)
2471#[link_section = "__interrupt_vector_10"]
2472#[no_mangle]
2473pub static TIM0_VECTOR: extern "msp430-interrupt" fn() = tim0;
2474
2475// The interrupt handler
2476extern "msp430-interrupt" fn tim0() {
2477    // ..
2478}
2479```

2487
2488Disassembly of section .text:
2489
24900000c000 <int::tim0>:
2491    c000:       00 13           reti
2492```

2507
2508When emitting PTX code, all vanilla Rust functions (`fn`) get translated to
2509"device" functions. These functions are *not* callable from the host via the
2510CUDA API so a crate with only device functions is not too useful!
2511
2512OTOH, "global" functions *can* be called by the host; you can think of them
2513as the real public API of your crate. To produce a global function use the
2514`"ptx-kernel"` ABI.
2515
2516<!-- NOTE(ignore) this example is specific to the nvptx targets -->
2517
2518``` rust,ignore
2519#![feature(abi_ptx)]
2520#![no_std]
2521
2522pub unsafe extern "ptx-kernel" fn global_function() {
2523    device_function();
2524}
2525
2526pub fn device_function() {
2527    // ..
2528}
2529```
2530
2531``` text
2532$ xargo rustc --target nvptx64-nvidia-cuda --release -- --emit=asm
2533
2534$ cat $(find -name '*.s')
2535//
2536// Generated by LLVM NVPTX Back-End
2537//
2538
2539.version 3.2
2540.target sm_20
2541.address_size 64
2542
2543        // .globl       _ZN6kernel15global_function17h46111ebe6516b382E
2544
2545.visible .entry _ZN6kernel15global_function17h46111ebe6516b382E()
2546{
2547
2548
2549        ret;
2550}
2551
2552        // .globl       _ZN6kernel15device_function17hd6a0e4993bbf3f78E
2553.visible .func _ZN6kernel15device_function17hd6a0e4993bbf3f78E()
2554{
2555
2556
2557        ret;
2558}
2559```

2729Allows for using more complex types for const parameters, such as structs or enums.
2730
2731```rust
2732#![feature(adt_const_params)]
2733#![allow(incomplete_features)]
2734
2735use std::marker::ConstParamTy;
2736
2737#[derive(ConstParamTy, PartialEq, Eq)]
2738enum Foo {
2739    A,
2740    B,
2741    C,
2742}
2743
2744#[derive(ConstParamTy, PartialEq, Eq)]
2745struct Bar {
2746    flag: bool,
2747}
2748
2749fn is_foo_a_and_bar_true<const F: Foo, const B: Bar>() -> bool {
2750    match (F, B.flag) {
2751        (Foo::A, true) => true,
2752        _ => false,
2753    }
2754}
2755```

2971------------------------
2972
2973Allows any type implementing `core::ops::Receiver<Target=T>` to be used as the type
2974of `self` in a method belonging to `T`.
2975
2976For example,
2977
2978```rust
2979#![feature(arbitrary_self_types)]
2980
2981struct A;
2982
2983impl A {
2984    fn f(self: SmartPtr<Self>) -> i32 { 1 }  // note self type
2985}
2986
2987struct SmartPtr<T>(T);
2988
2989impl<T> core::ops::Receiver for SmartPtr<T> {
2990    type Target = T;
2991}
2992
2993fn main() {
2994    let smart_ptr = SmartPtr(A);
2995    assert_eq!(smart_ptr.f(), 1);
2996}
2997```
2998
2999The `Receiver` trait has a blanket implementation for all `T: Deref`, so in fact
3000things like this work too:
3001
3002```rust
3003#![feature(arbitrary_self_types)]
3004
3005use std::rc::Rc;
3006
3007struct A;
3008
3009impl A {
3010    fn f(self: Rc<Self>) -> i32 { 1 } // Rc implements Deref
3011}
3012
3013fn main() {
3014    let smart_ptr = Rc::new(A);
3015    assert_eq!(smart_ptr.f(), 1);
3016}
3017```
3018
3019Interestingly, that works even without the `arbitrary_self_types` feature
3020- but that's because certain types are _effectively_ hard coded, including
3021`Rc`. ("Hard coding" isn't quite true; they use a lang-item called
3022`LegacyReceiver` to denote their special-ness in this way). With the
3023`arbitrary_self_types` feature, their special-ness goes away, and custom
3024smart pointers can achieve the same.
3025
3026## Changes to method lookup
3027
3028Method lookup previously used to work by stepping through the `Deref`
3029chain then using the resulting list of steps in two different ways:
3030
3031* To identify types that might contribute methods via their `impl`
3032  blocks (inherent methods) or via traits
3033* To identify the types that the method receiver (`a` in the above
3034  examples) can be converted to.
3035
3036With this feature, these lists are created by instead stepping through
3037the `Receiver` chain. However, a note is kept about whether the type
3038can be reached also via the `Deref` chain.
3039
3040The full chain (via `Receiver` hops) is used for the first purpose
3041(identifying relevant `impl` blocks and traits); whereas the shorter
3042list (reachable via `Deref`) is used for the second purpose. That's
3043because, to convert the method target (`a` in `a.b()`) to the self
3044type, Rust may need to be able to use `Deref::deref`. Type conversions,
3045then, can only proceed as far as the end of the `Deref` chain whereas
3046the longer `Receiver` chain can be used to explore more places where
3047useful methods might reside.
3048
3049## Types suitable for use as smart pointers
3050
3051This feature allows the creation of customised smart pointers - for example
3052your own equivalent to `Rc` or `Box` with whatever capabilities you like.
3053Those smart pointers can either implement `Deref` (if it's safe to
3054create a reference to the referent) or `Receiver` (if it isn't).
3055
3056Either way, smart pointer types should mostly _avoid having methods_.
3057Calling methods on a smart pointer leads to ambiguity about whether you're
3058aiming for a method on the pointer, or on the referent.
3059
3060Best practice is therefore to put smart pointer functionality into
3061associated functions instead - that's what's done in all the smart pointer
3062types within Rust's standard library which implement `Receiver`.
3063
3064If you choose to add any methods to your smart pointer type, your users
3065may run into errors from deshadowing, as described in the next section.
3066
3067## Avoiding shadowing
3068
3069With or without this feature, Rust emits an error if it finds two method
3070candidates, like this:
3071
3072```rust,compile_fail
3073use std::pin::Pin;
3074use std::pin::pin;
3075
3076struct A;
3077
3078impl A {
3079    fn get_ref(self: Pin<&A>) {}
3080}
3081
3082fn main() {
3083    let pinned_a: Pin<&A> = pin!(A).as_ref();
3084    let pinned_a: Pin<&A> = pinned_a.as_ref();
3085    pinned_a.get_ref(); // error[E0034]: multiple applicable items in scope
3086}
3087```
3088
3089(this is why Rust's smart pointers are mostly carefully designed to avoid
3090having methods at all, and shouldn't add new methods in future.)
3091
3092With `arbitrary_self_types`, we take care to spot some other kinds of
3093conflict:
3094
3095```rust,compile_fail
3096#![feature(arbitrary_self_types)]
3097
3098use std::pin::Pin;
3099use std::pin::pin;
3100
3101struct A;
3102
3103impl A {
3104    fn get_ref(self: &Pin<&A>) {}  // note &Pin
3105}
3106
3107fn main() {
3108    let pinned_a: Pin<&mut A> = pin!(A);
3109    let pinned_a: Pin<&A> = pinned_a.as_ref();
3110    pinned_a.get_ref();
3111}
3112```
3113
3114This is to guard against the case where an inner (referent) type has a
3115method of a given name, taking the smart pointer by reference, and then
3116the smart pointer implementer adds a similar method taking self by value.
3117As noted in the previous section, the safe option is simply
3118not to add methods to smart pointers, and then these errors can't occur.

3134This extends the [arbitrary self types] feature to allow methods to

3140struct A;
3141
3142impl A {
3143    fn m(self: *const Self) {}
3144}
3145
3146fn main() {
3147    let a = A;
3148    let a_ptr: *const A = &a as *const A;
3149    a_ptr.m();
3150}
3151```
3152
3153In general this is not advised: it's thought to be better practice to wrap
3154raw pointers in a newtype wrapper which implements the `core::ops::Receiver`
3155trait, then you need "only" the `arbitrary_self_types` feature. For example:
3156
3157```rust
3158#![feature(arbitrary_self_types)]
3159#![allow(dead_code)]
3160
3161struct A;
3162
3163impl A {
3164    fn m(self: Wrapper<Self>) {} // can extract the pointer and do
3165        // what it needs
3166}
3167
3168struct Wrapper<T>(*const T);
3169
3170impl<T> core::ops::Receiver for Wrapper<T> {
3171    type Target = T;
3172}
3173
3174fn main() {
3175    let a = A;
3176    let a_ptr: *const A = &a as *const A;
3177    let a_wrapper = Wrapper(a_ptr);
3178    a_wrapper.m();
3179}
3180```
3181
3182[arbitrary self types]: arbitrary-self-types.md

3342This feature tracks `asm!` and `global_asm!` support for the following architectures:
3343- NVPTX
3344- Hexagon
3345- MIPS32r2 and MIPS64r2
3346- wasm32
3347- BPF
3348- SPIR-V
3349- AVR
3350- MSP430
3351- M68k
3352- CSKY
3353- SPARC
3354- Xtensa
3355
3356## Register classes
3357
3358| Architecture | Register class | Registers                          | LLVM constraint code |
3359| ------------ | -------------- | ---------------------------------- | -------------------- |
3360| MIPS         | `reg`          | `$[2-25]`                          | `r`                  |
3361| MIPS         | `freg`         | `$f[0-31]`                         | `f`                  |
3362| NVPTX        | `reg16`        | None\*                             | `h`                  |
3363| NVPTX        | `reg32`        | None\*                             | `r`                  |
3364| NVPTX        | `reg64`        | None\*                             | `l`                  |
3365| Hexagon      | `reg`          | `r[0-28]`                          | `r`                  |
3366| Hexagon      | `preg`         | `p[0-3]`                           | Only clobbers        |
3367| wasm32       | `local`        | None\*                             | `r`                  |
3368| BPF          | `reg`          | `r[0-10]`                          | `r`                  |
3369| BPF          | `wreg`         | `w[0-10]`                          | `w`                  |
3370| AVR          | `reg`          | `r[2-25]`, `XH`, `XL`, `ZH`, `ZL`  | `r`                  |
3371| AVR          | `reg_upper`    | `r[16-25]`, `XH`, `XL`, `ZH`, `ZL` | `d`                  |
3372| AVR          | `reg_pair`     | `r3r2` .. `r25r24`, `X`, `Z`       | `r`                  |
3373| AVR          | `reg_iw`       | `r25r24`, `X`, `Z`                 | `w`                  |
3374| AVR          | `reg_ptr`      | `X`, `Z`                           | `e`                  |
3375| MSP430       | `reg`          | `r[0-15]`                          | `r`                  |
3376| M68k         | `reg`          | `d[0-7]`, `a[0-7]`                 | `r`                  |
3377| M68k         | `reg_data`     | `d[0-7]`                           | `d`                  |
3378| M68k         | `reg_addr`     | `a[0-3]`                           | `a`                  |
3379| CSKY         | `reg`          | `r[0-31]`                          | `r`                  |
3380| CSKY         | `freg`         | `f[0-31]`                          | `f`                  |
3381| SPARC        | `reg`          | `r[2-29]`                          | `r`                  |
3382| SPARC        | `yreg`         | `y`                                | Only clobbers        |
3383| Xtensa       | `reg`          | `a[2-15]`                          | `r`                  |
3384| Xtensa       | `freg`         | `f[0-15]`                          | `f`                  |
3385| Xtensa       | `sreg`         | `sar`, `scompare1`, `lbeg`, `lend`, `lcount`, `acclo`, `acchi`, `m[0-3]` | Only clobbers |
3386| Xtensa       | `breg`         | `b[0-15]`                          | Only clobbers        |
3387
3388> **Notes**:
3389> - NVPTX doesn't have a fixed register set, so named registers are not supported.
3390>
3391> - WebAssembly doesn't have registers, so named registers are not supported.

3464## Unsupported registers
3465
3466| Architecture | Unsupported register                    | Reason                                                                                                                                                                              |
3467| ------------ | --------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
3468| All          | `sp`, `r14`/`o6` (SPARC)                | The stack pointer must be restored to its original value at the end of an asm code block.                                                                                           |
3469| All          | `fr` (Hexagon) `$fp` (MIPS), `Y` (AVR), `r4` (MSP430), `a6` (M68k), `r30`/`i6` (SPARC) | The frame pointer cannot be used as an input or output.                                                             |
3470| All          | `r19` (Hexagon) | These are used internally by LLVM as "base pointer" for functions with complex stack frames.                                                                              |
3471| MIPS         | `$0` or `$zero`                         | This is a constant zero register which can't be modified.                                                                                                                           |
3472| MIPS         | `$1` or `$at`                           | Reserved for assembler.                                                                                                                                                             |
3473| MIPS         | `$26`/`$k0`, `$27`/`$k1`                | OS-reserved registers.                                                                                                                                                              |
3474| MIPS         | `$28`/`$gp`                             | Global pointer cannot be used as inputs or outputs.                                                                                                                                 |
3475| MIPS         | `$ra`                                   | Return address cannot be used as inputs or outputs.                                                                                                                                 |
3476| Hexagon      | `lr`                                    | This is the link register which cannot be used as an input or output.                                                                                                               |
3477| AVR          | `r0`, `r1`, `r1r0`                      | Due to an issue in LLVM, the `r0` and `r1` registers cannot be used as inputs or outputs.  If modified, they must be restored to their original values before the end of the block. |
3478|MSP430        | `r0`, `r2`, `r3`                        | These are the program counter, status register, and constant generator respectively. Neither the status register nor constant generator can be written to.                          |
3479| M68k         | `a4`, `a5`                              | Used internally by LLVM for the base pointer and global base pointer. |
3480| CSKY         | `r7`, `r28`                             | Used internally by LLVM for the base pointer and global base pointer. |
3481| CSKY         | `r8`                                    | Used internally by LLVM for the frame pointer. |
3482| CSKY         | `r14`                                   | Used internally by LLVM for the stack pointer. |
3483| CSKY         | `r15`                                   | This is the link register. |
3484| CSKY         | `r[26-30]`                              | Reserved by its ABI.       |
3485| CSKY         | `r31`                                   | This is the TLS register.  |
3486| SPARC        | `r0`/`g0`                               | This is always zero and cannot be used as inputs or outputs. |
3487| SPARC        | `r1`/`g1`                               | Used internally by LLVM. |
3488| SPARC        | `r5`/`g5`                               | Reserved for system. (SPARC32 only) |
3489| SPARC        | `r6`/`g6`, `r7`/`g7`                    | Reserved for system. |
3490| SPARC        | `r31`/`i7`                              | Return address cannot be used as inputs or outputs. |
3491| Xtensa       | `a0`                                    | This is the return address register and is used internally by LLVM. |
3492| Xtensa       | `a1`/`sp`                               | This is the stack pointer and is used internally by LLVM. |
3493| Xtensa       | `a7` (windowed ABI) / `a15` (call0 ABI) | The frame pointer cannot be used as an input or output. |

3512# Flags covered by `preserves_flags`
3513
3514These flags registers must be restored upon exiting the asm block if the `preserves_flags` option is set:
3515- AVR
3516  - The status register `SREG`.
3517- MSP430
3518  - The status register `r2`.
3519- M68k
3520  - The condition code register `ccr`.
3521- SPARC
3522  - Integer condition codes (`icc` and `xcc`)
3523  - Floating-point condition codes (`fcc[0-3]`)
3524- CSKY
3525  - Condition/carry bit (C) in `PSR`.

3599This feature allows label operands to be used together with output operands.
3600
3601Example:
3602```rust,ignore (partial-example, x86-only)
3603
3604unsafe {
3605    let a: usize;
3606    asm!(
3607        "mov {}, 1"
3608        "jmp {}",
3609        out(reg) a,
3610        label {
3611            println!("Jumped from asm {}!", a);
3612        }
3613    );
3614}
3615```
3616
3617The output operands are assigned before the label blocks are executed.

3710
3711The `async_fn_traits` feature allows for implementation of the [`AsyncFn*`] traits
3712for creating custom closure-like types that return futures.
3713

3715
3716The main difference to the `Fn*` family of traits is that `AsyncFn` can return a future
3717that borrows from itself (`FnOnce::Output` has no lifetime parameters, while `AsyncFnMut::CallRefFuture` does).

3855----
3856
3857The `auto_traits` feature gate allows you to define auto traits.
3858
3859Auto traits, like [`Send`] or [`Sync`] in the standard library, are marker traits
3860that are automatically implemented for every type, unless the type, or a type it contains,
3861has explicitly opted out via a negative impl. (Negative impls are separately controlled
3862by the `negative_impls` feature.)
3863
3864[`Send`]: ../../std/marker/trait.Send.html
3865[`Sync`]: ../../std/marker/trait.Sync.html
3866
3867```rust,ignore (partial-example)
3868impl !Trait for Type {}
3869```
3870
3871Example:
3872
3873```rust
3874#![feature(negative_impls)]
3875#![feature(auto_traits)]
3876
3877auto trait Valid {}
3878
3879struct True;
3880struct False;
3881
3882impl !Valid for False {}
3883
3884struct MaybeValid<T>(T);
3885
3886fn must_be_valid<T: Valid>(_t: T) { }
3887
3888fn main() {
3889    // works
3890    must_be_valid( MaybeValid(True) );
3891
3892    // compiler error - trait bound not satisfied
3893    // must_be_valid( MaybeValid(False) );
3894}
3895```
3896
3897## Automatic trait implementations
3898
3899When a type is declared as an `auto trait`, we will automatically
3900create impls for every struct/enum/union, unless an explicit impl is
3901provided. These automatic impls contain a where clause for each field
3902of the form `T: AutoTrait`, where `T` is the type of the field and
3903`AutoTrait` is the auto trait in question. As an example, consider the
3904struct `List` and the auto trait `Send`:
3905
3906```rust
3907struct List<T> {
3908  data: T,
3909  next: Option<Box<List<T>>>,
3910}
3911```
3912
3913Presuming that there is no explicit impl of `Send` for `List`, the
3914compiler will supply an automatic impl of the form:
3915
3916```rust
3917struct List<T> {
3918  data: T,
3919  next: Option<Box<List<T>>>,
3920}
3921
3922unsafe impl<T> Send for List<T>
3923where
3924  T: Send, // from the field `data`
3925  Option<Box<List<T>>>: Send, // from the field `next`
3926{ }
3927```
3928
3929Explicit impls may be either positive or negative. They take the form:
3930
3931```rust,ignore (partial-example)
3932impl<...> AutoTrait for StructName<..> { }
3933impl<...> !AutoTrait for StructName<..> { }
3934```
3935
3936## Coinduction: Auto traits permit cyclic matching
3937
3938Unlike ordinary trait matching, auto traits are **coinductive**. This
3939means, in short, that cycles which occur in trait matching are
3940considered ok. As an example, consider the recursive struct `List`
3941introduced in the previous section. In attempting to determine whether
3942`List: Send`, we would wind up in a cycle: to apply the impl, we must
3943show that `Option<Box<List>>: Send`, which will in turn require
3944`Box<List>: Send` and then finally `List: Send` again. Under ordinary
3945trait matching, this cycle would be an error, but for an auto trait it
3946is considered a successful match.
3947
3948## Items
3949
3950Auto traits cannot have any trait items, such as methods or associated types. This ensures that we can generate default implementations.
3951
3952## Supertraits
3953
3954Auto traits cannot have supertraits. This is for soundness reasons, as the interaction of coinduction with implied bounds is difficult to reconcile.

4678------------------------
4679
4680The `cfg_sanitize` feature makes it possible to execute different code
4681depending on whether a particular sanitizer is enabled or not.
4682
4683## Examples
4684
4685```rust
4686#![feature(cfg_sanitize)]
4687
4688#[cfg(sanitize = "thread")]
4689fn a() {
4690    // ...
4691}
4692
4693#[cfg(not(sanitize = "thread"))]
4694fn a() {
4695    // ...
4696}
4697
4698fn b() {
4699    if cfg!(sanitize = "leak") {
4700        // ...
4701    } else {
4702        // ...
4703    }
4704}
4705```

4826    // ...
4827}
4828
4829fn b() {
4830    if cfg!(target_object_format = "wasm") {
4831        // ...
4832    } else {
4833        // ...
4834    }
4835}

4882------------------------
4883
4884The `cfg_version` feature makes it possible to execute different code
4885depending on the compiler version. It will return true if the compiler
4886version is greater than or equal to the specified version.
4887
4888## Examples
4889
4890```rust
4891#![feature(cfg_version)]
4892
4893#[cfg(version("1.42"))] // 1.42 and above
4894fn a() {
4895    // ...
4896}
4897
4898#[cfg(not(version("1.42")))] // 1.41 and below
4899fn a() {
4900    // ...
4901}
4902
4903fn b() {
4904    if cfg!(version("1.42")) {
4905        // ...
4906    } else {
4907        // ...
4908    }
4909}
4910```

4919
4920The tracking issue for this feature is: [#89653]
4921
4922[#89653]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/89653
4923
4924------------------------
4925
4926The `cfi_encoding` feature allows the user to define a CFI encoding for a type.
4927It allows the user to use a different names for types that otherwise would be
4928required to have the same name as used in externally defined C functions.
4929
4930## Examples
4931
4932```rust
4933#![feature(cfi_encoding, extern_types)]
4934
4935#[cfi_encoding = "3Foo"]
4936pub struct Type1(i32);
4937
4938extern {
4939    #[cfi_encoding = "3Bar"]
4940    type Type2;
4941}
4942```

5217for targets with the Armv8-M architecture profile (`thumbv8m` in their target
5218name).
5219LLVM, the Rust compiler and the linker are providing
5220[support](https://developer.arm.com/documentation/ecm0359818/latest/) for the
5221TrustZone-M feature.
5222
5223One of the things provided with this unstable feature is the "cmse-nonsecure-entry" ABI.
5224This ABI marks a Secure function as an entry function (see
5225[section 5.4](https://developer.arm.com/documentation/ecm0359818/latest/) for details).
5226With this ABI, the compiler will do the following:
5227* add a special symbol on the function which is the `__acle_se_` prefix and the
5228  standard function name
5229* constrain the number of parameters to avoid using the Non-Secure stack
5230* before returning from the function, clear registers that might contain Secure
5231  information
5232* use the `BXNS` instruction to return
5233
5234Because the stack can not be used to pass parameters, there will be compilation
5235errors if:
5236* the total size of all parameters is too big (for example, more than four 32-bit integers)
5237
5238The special symbol `__acle_se_` will be used by the linker to generate a secure
5239gateway veneer.
5240
5241<!-- NOTE(ignore) this example is specific to thumbv8m targets -->
5242
5243``` rust,ignore
5244#![no_std]
5245#![feature(cmse_nonsecure_entry)]
5246
5247#[no_mangle]
5248pub extern "cmse-nonsecure-entry" fn entry_function(input: u32) -> u32 {
5249    input + 6
5250}
5251```
5252
5253``` text
5254$ rustc --emit obj --crate-type lib --target thumbv8m.main-none-eabi function.rs
5255$ arm-none-eabi-objdump -D function.o

5258   0:   b580            push    {r7, lr}

5260   4:   b082            sub     sp, #8

5262   8:   1d81            adds    r1, r0, #6
5263   a:   460a            mov     r2, r1
5264   c:   4281            cmp     r1, r0
5265   e:   9200            str     r2, [sp, #0]
5266  10:   d30b            bcc.n   2a <entry_function+0x2a>
5267  12:   e7ff            b.n     14 <entry_function+0x14>
5268  14:   9800            ldr     r0, [sp, #0]
5269  16:   b002            add     sp, #8
5270  18:   e8bd 4080       ldmia.w sp!, {r7, lr}
5271  1c:   4671            mov     r1, lr
5272  1e:   4672            mov     r2, lr
5273  20:   4673            mov     r3, lr
5274  22:   46f4            mov     ip, lr
5275  24:   f38e 8800       msr     CPSR_f, lr
5276  28:   4774            bxns    lr
5277  2a:   f240 0000       movw    r0, #0
5278  2e:   f2c0 0000       movt    r0, #0
5279  32:   f240 0200       movw    r2, #0

6492------------------------
6493
6494The `coroutines` feature gate in Rust allows you to define coroutine or
6495coroutine literals. A coroutine is a "resumable function" that syntactically
6496resembles a closure but compiles to much different semantics in the compiler
6497itself. The primary feature of a coroutine is that it can be suspended during
6498execution to be resumed at a later date. Coroutines use the `yield` keyword to
6499"return", and then the caller can `resume` a coroutine to resume execution just
6500after the `yield` keyword.
6501
6502Coroutines are an extra-unstable feature in the compiler right now. Added in
6503[RFC 2033] they're mostly intended right now as a information/constraint
6504gathering phase. The intent is that experimentation can happen on the nightly
6505compiler before actual stabilization. A further RFC will be required to
6506stabilize coroutines and will likely contain at least a few small
6507tweaks to the overall design.
6508
6509[RFC 2033]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rfcs/pull/2033
6510
6511A syntactical example of a coroutine is:
6512
6513```rust
6514#![feature(coroutines, coroutine_trait, stmt_expr_attributes)]
6515
6516use std::ops::{Coroutine, CoroutineState};
6517use std::pin::Pin;
6518
6519fn main() {
6520    let mut coroutine = #[coroutine] || {
6521        yield 1;
6522        return "foo"
6523    };
6524
6525    match Pin::new(&mut coroutine).resume(()) {
6526        CoroutineState::Yielded(1) => {}
6527        _ => panic!("unexpected value from resume"),
6528    }
6529    match Pin::new(&mut coroutine).resume(()) {
6530        CoroutineState::Complete("foo") => {}
6531        _ => panic!("unexpected value from resume"),
6532    }
6533}
6534```
6535
6536Coroutines are closure-like literals which are annotated with `#[coroutine]`
6537and can contain a `yield` statement. The
6538`yield` statement takes an optional expression of a value to yield out of the
6539coroutine. All coroutine literals implement the `Coroutine` trait in the
6540`std::ops` module. The `Coroutine` trait has one main method, `resume`, which
6541resumes execution of the coroutine at the previous suspension point.
6542
6543An example of the control flow of coroutines is that the following example
6544prints all numbers in order:
6545
6546```rust
6547#![feature(coroutines, coroutine_trait, stmt_expr_attributes)]
6548
6549use std::ops::Coroutine;
6550use std::pin::Pin;
6551
6552fn main() {
6553    let mut coroutine = #[coroutine] || {
6554        println!("2");
6555        yield;
6556        println!("4");
6557    };
6558
6559    println!("1");
6560    Pin::new(&mut coroutine).resume(());
6561    println!("3");
6562    Pin::new(&mut coroutine).resume(());
6563    println!("5");
6564}
6565```
6566
6567At this time the main use case of coroutines is an implementation
6568primitive for `async`/`await` and `gen` syntax, but coroutines
6569will likely be extended to other primitives in the future.
6570Feedback on the design and usage is always appreciated!
6571
6572### The `Coroutine` trait
6573
6574The `Coroutine` trait in `std::ops` currently looks like:
6575
6576```rust
6577# #![feature(arbitrary_self_types, coroutine_trait)]
6578# use std::ops::CoroutineState;
6579# use std::pin::Pin;
6580
6581pub trait Coroutine<R = ()> {
6582    type Yield;
6583    type Return;
6584    fn resume(self: Pin<&mut Self>, resume: R) -> CoroutineState<Self::Yield, Self::Return>;
6585}
6586```
6587
6588The `Coroutine::Yield` type is the type of values that can be yielded with the
6589`yield` statement. The `Coroutine::Return` type is the returned type of the
6590coroutine. This is typically the last expression in a coroutine's definition or
6591any value passed to `return` in a coroutine. The `resume` function is the entry
6592point for executing the `Coroutine` itself.
6593
6594The return value of `resume`, `CoroutineState`, looks like:
6595
6596```rust
6597pub enum CoroutineState<Y, R> {
6598    Yielded(Y),
6599    Complete(R),
6600}
6601```
6602
6603The `Yielded` variant indicates that the coroutine can later be resumed. This
6604corresponds to a `yield` point in a coroutine. The `Complete` variant indicates
6605that the coroutine is complete and cannot be resumed again. Calling `resume`
6606after a coroutine has returned `Complete` will likely result in a panic of the
6607program.
6608
6609### Closure-like semantics
6610
6611The closure-like syntax for coroutines alludes to the fact that they also have
6612closure-like semantics. Namely:
6613
6614* When created, a coroutine executes no code. A closure literal does not
6615  actually execute any of the closure's code on construction, and similarly a
6616  coroutine literal does not execute any code inside the coroutine when
6617  constructed.
6618
6619* Coroutines can capture outer variables by reference or by move, and this can
6620  be tweaked with the `move` keyword at the beginning of the closure. Like
6621  closures all coroutines will have an implicit environment which is inferred by
6622  the compiler. Outer variables can be moved into a coroutine for use as the
6623  coroutine progresses.
6624
6625* Coroutine literals produce a value with a unique type which implements the
6626  `std::ops::Coroutine` trait. This allows actual execution of the coroutine
6627  through the `Coroutine::resume` method as well as also naming it in return
6628  types and such.
6629
6630* Traits like `Send` and `Sync` are automatically implemented for a `Coroutine`
6631  depending on the captured variables of the environment. Unlike closures,
6632  coroutines also depend on variables live across suspension points. This means
6633  that although the ambient environment may be `Send` or `Sync`, the coroutine
6634  itself may not be due to internal variables live across `yield` points being
6635  not-`Send` or not-`Sync`. Note that coroutines do
6636  not implement traits like `Copy` or `Clone` automatically.
6637
6638* Whenever a coroutine is dropped it will drop all captured environment
6639  variables.
6640
6641### Coroutines as state machines
6642
6643In the compiler, coroutines are currently compiled as state machines. Each
6644`yield` expression will correspond to a different state that stores all live
6645variables over that suspension point. Resumption of a coroutine will dispatch on
6646the current state and then execute internally until a `yield` is reached, at
6647which point all state is saved off in the coroutine and a value is returned.
6648
6649Let's take a look at an example to see what's going on here:
6650
6651```rust
6652#![feature(coroutines, coroutine_trait, stmt_expr_attributes)]
6653
6654use std::ops::Coroutine;
6655use std::pin::Pin;
6656
6657fn main() {
6658    let ret = "foo";
6659    let mut coroutine = #[coroutine] move || {
6660        yield 1;
6661        return ret
6662    };
6663
6664    Pin::new(&mut coroutine).resume(());
6665    Pin::new(&mut coroutine).resume(());
6666}
6667```
6668
6669This coroutine literal will compile down to something similar to:
6670
6671```rust
6672#![feature(arbitrary_self_types, coroutine_trait)]
6673
6674use std::ops::{Coroutine, CoroutineState};
6675use std::pin::Pin;
6676
6677fn main() {
6678    let ret = "foo";
6679    let mut coroutine = {
6680        enum __Coroutine {
6681            Start(&'static str),
6682            Yield1(&'static str),
6683            Done,
6684        }
6685
6686        impl Coroutine for __Coroutine {
6687            type Yield = i32;
6688            type Return = &'static str;
6689
6690            fn resume(mut self: Pin<&mut Self>, resume: ()) -> CoroutineState<i32, &'static str> {
6691                use std::mem;
6692                match mem::replace(&mut *self, __Coroutine::Done) {
6693                    __Coroutine::Start(s) => {
6694                        *self = __Coroutine::Yield1(s);
6695                        CoroutineState::Yielded(1)
6696                    }
6697
6698                    __Coroutine::Yield1(s) => {
6699                        *self = __Coroutine::Done;
6700                        CoroutineState::Complete(s)
6701                    }
6702
6703                    __Coroutine::Done => {
6704                        panic!("coroutine resumed after completion")
6705                    }
6706                }
6707            }
6708        }
6709
6710        __Coroutine::Start(ret)
6711    };
6712
6713    Pin::new(&mut coroutine).resume(());
6714    Pin::new(&mut coroutine).resume(());
6715}
6716```
6717
6718Notably here we can see that the compiler is generating a fresh type,
6719`__Coroutine` in this case. This type has a number of states (represented here
6720as an `enum`) corresponding to each of the conceptual states of the coroutine.
6721At the beginning we're closing over our outer variable `foo` and then that
6722variable is also live over the `yield` point, so it's stored in both states.
6723
6724When the coroutine starts it'll immediately yield 1, but it saves off its state
6725just before it does so indicating that it has reached the yield point. Upon
6726resuming again we'll execute the `return ret` which returns the `Complete`
6727state.
6728
6729Here we can also note that the `Done` state, if resumed, panics immediately as
6730it's invalid to resume a completed coroutine. It's also worth noting that this
6731is just a rough desugaring, not a normative specification for what the compiler
6732does.

6762---
6763
6764The `coverage` attribute can be used to selectively disable coverage
6765instrumentation in an annotated function. This might be useful to:
6766
6767-   Avoid instrumentation overhead in a performance critical function
6768-   Avoid generating coverage for a function that is not meant to be executed,
6769    but still target 100% coverage for the rest of the program.
6770
6771## Example
6772
6773```rust
6774#![feature(coverage_attribute)]
6775
6776// `foo()` will get coverage instrumentation (by default)
6777fn foo() {
6778  // ...
6779}
6780
6781#[coverage(off)]
6782fn bar() {
6783  // ...
6784}
6785```

6924
6925The `custom_test_frameworks` feature allows the use of `#[test_case]` and `#![test_runner]`.
6926Any function, const, or static can be annotated with `#[test_case]` causing it to be aggregated (like `#[test]`)
6927and be passed to the test runner determined by the `#![test_runner]` crate attribute.
6928
6929```rust
6930#![feature(custom_test_frameworks)]
6931#![test_runner(my_runner)]
6932
6933fn my_runner(tests: &[&i32]) {
6934    for t in tests {
6935        if **t == 0 {
6936            println!("PASSED");
6937        } else {
6938            println!("FAILED");
6939        }
6940    }
6941}
6942
6943#[test_case]
6944const WILL_PASS: i32 = 0;
6945
6946#[test_case]
6947const WILL_FAIL: i32 = 4;
6948```

7025
7026------------------------
7027
7028The `default_field_values` feature allows users to specify a const value for
7029individual fields in struct definitions, allowing those to be omitted from
7030initializers.
7031
7032## Examples
7033
7034```rust
7035#![feature(default_field_values)]
7036
7037#[derive(Default)]
7038struct Pet {
7039    name: Option<String>, // impl Default for Pet will use Default::default() for name
7040    age: i128 = 42, // impl Default for Pet will use the literal 42 for age
7041}
7042
7043fn main() {
7044    let a = Pet { name: Some(String::new()), .. }; // Pet { name: Some(""), age: 42 }
7045    let b = Pet::default(); // Pet { name: None, age: 42 }
7046    assert_eq!(a.age, b.age);
7047    // The following would be a compilation error: `name` needs to be specified
7048    // let _ = Pet { .. };
7049}
7050```
7051
7052## `#[derive(Default)]`
7053
7054When deriving Default, the provided values are then used. On enum variants,
7055the variant must still be marked with `#[default]` and have all its fields
7056with default values.
7057
7058```rust
7059#![feature(default_field_values)]
7060
7061#[derive(Default)]
7062enum A {
7063    #[default]
7064    B {
7065        x: i32 = 0,
7066        y: i32 = 0,
7067    },
7068    C,
7069}
7070```
7071
7072## Enum variants
7073
7074This feature also supports enum variants for both specifying default values
7075and `#[derive(Default)]`.
7076
7077## Interaction with `#[non_exhaustive]`
7078
7079A struct or enum variant marked with `#[non_exhaustive]` is not allowed to
7080have default field values.
7081
7082## Lints
7083
7084When manually implementing the `Default` trait for a type that has default
7085field values, if any of these are overridden in the impl the
7086`default_overrides_default_fields` lint will trigger. This lint is in place
7087to avoid surprising diverging behavior between `S { .. }` and
7088`S::default()`, where using the same type in both ways could result in
7089different values. The appropriate way to write a manual `Default`
7090implementation is to use the functional update syntax:
7091
7092```rust
7093#![feature(default_field_values)]
7094
7095struct Pet {
7096    name: String,
7097    age: i128 = 42, // impl Default for Pet will use the literal 42 for age
7098}
7099
7100impl Default for Pet {
7101    fn default() -> Pet {
7102        Pet {
7103            name: "no-name".to_string(),
7104            ..
7105        }
7106    }
7107}
7108```

7170------------------------
7171
7172> **Note**: This feature supersedes `box_patterns`.
7173
7174This feature permits pattern matching on [smart pointers in the standard library] through their
7175`Deref` target types, either implicitly or with explicit `deref!(_)` patterns (the syntax of which
7176is currently a placeholder).
7177
7178```rust
7179#![feature(deref_patterns)]
7180
7181let mut v = vec![Box::new(Some(0))];
7182
7183// Implicit dereferences are inserted when a pattern can match against the
7184// result of repeatedly dereferencing but can't match against a smart
7185// pointer itself. This works alongside match ergonomics for references.
7186if let [Some(x)] = &mut v {
7187    *x += 1;
7188}
7189
7190// Explicit `deref!(_)` patterns may instead be used when finer control is
7191// needed, e.g. to dereference only a single smart pointer, or to bind the
7192// the result of dereferencing to a variable.
7193if let deref!([deref!(opt_x @ Some(1))]) = &mut v {
7194    opt_x.as_mut().map(|x| *x += 1);
7195}
7196
7197assert_eq!(v, [Box::new(Some(2))]);
7198```
7199
7200Without this feature, it may be necessary to introduce temporaries to represent dereferenced places
7201when matching on nested structures:
7202
7203```rust
7204let mut v = vec![Box::new(Some(0))];
7205if let [b] = &mut *v {
7206    if let Some(x) = &mut **b {
7207        *x += 1;
7208    }
7209}
7210if let [b] = &mut *v {
7211    if let opt_x @ Some(1) = &mut **b {
7212        opt_x.as_mut().map(|x| *x += 1);
7213    }
7214}
7215assert_eq!(v, [Box::new(Some(2))]);
7216```
7217
7218Deref patterns may move out of boxes:
7219
7220```rust
7221# #![feature(deref_patterns)]
7222struct NoCopy;
7223let deref!(x) = Box::new(NoCopy);
7224drop::<NoCopy>(x);
7225```
7226
7227Additionally, `deref_patterns` implements changes to string and byte string literal patterns,
7228allowing then to be used in deref patterns:
7229
7230```rust
7231# #![feature(deref_patterns)]
7232match ("test".to_string(), Box::from("test"), b"test".to_vec()) {
7233    ("test", "test", b"test") => {}
7234    _ => panic!(),
7235}
7236
7237// This works through multiple layers of reference and smart pointer:
7238match (&Box::new(&"test".to_string()), &&&"test") {
7239    ("test", "test") => {}
7240    _ => panic!(),
7241}
7242
7243// `deref!("...")` syntax may also be used:
7244match "test".to_string() {
7245    deref!("test") => {}
7246    _ => panic!(),
7247}
7248
7249// Matching on slices and arrays using literals is possible elsewhere as well:
7250match *"test" {
7251    "test" => {}
7252    _ => panic!(),
7253}
7254match *b"test" {
7255    b"test" => {}
7256    _ => panic!(),
7257}
7258match *(b"test" as &[u8]) {
7259    b"test" => {}
7260    _ => panic!(),
7261}
7262```
7263
7264[smart pointers in the standard library]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/ops/trait.DerefPure.html#implementors

7396------------------------
7397
7398The `diagnostic_on_move` feature allows use of the `#[diagnostic::on_move]` attribute. It should be
7399placed on struct, enum and union declarations, though it is not an error to be located in other
7400positions. This attribute is a hint to the compiler to supplement the error message when the
7401annotated type is involved in a borrowcheck error.
7402
7403For example, [`File`] is annotated as such:
7404```rust
7405#![feature(diagnostic_on_move)]
7406
7407#[diagnostic::on_move(note = "you can use `File::try_clone` \
7408                             to duplicate a `File` instance")]
7409pub struct File {
7410    // ...
7411}
7412```
7413
7414When you try to use a `File` after it's already been moved, it will helpfully tell you about `try_clone`.
7415
7416The message and label can also be customized:
7417
7418```rust
7419#![feature(diagnostic_on_move)]
7420
7421use std::marker::PhantomData;
7422
7423#[diagnostic::on_move(
7424    message = "`{Self}` cannot be used multiple times",
7425    label = "this token may only be used once",
7426    note = "you can create a new `Token` with `Token::conjure()`"
7427)]
7428pub struct Token<'brand> {
7429    spooky: PhantomData<&'brand ()>,
7430}
7431
7432impl Token<'_> {
7433    pub fn conjure<'u>() -> Token<'u> {
7434        Token {
7435            spooky: PhantomData,
7436        }
7437    }
7438}
7439```
7440The user may try to use it like this:
7441```rust,compile_fail,E0382
7442# #![feature(diagnostic_on_move)]
7443#
7444# use std::marker::PhantomData;
7445#
7446# #[diagnostic::on_move(
7447#     message = "`{Self}` cannot be used multiple times",
7448#     label = "this token may only be used once",
7449#     note = "you can create a new `Token` with `Token::conjure()`"
7450# )]
7451# pub struct Token<'brand> {
7452#     spooky: PhantomData<&'brand ()>,
7453# }
7454#
7455# impl Token<'_> {
7456#     pub fn conjure<'u>() -> Token<'u> {
7457#         Token {
7458#             spooky: PhantomData,
7459#         }
7460#     }
7461# }
7462# fn main() {
7463let token = Token::conjure();
7464let _ = (token, token);
7465# }
7466```
7467This will result in the following error:
7468```text
7469error[E0382]: `Token` cannot be used multiple times
7470  --> src/main.rs:24:21
7471   |
7472 1 |     let token = Token::conjure();
7473   |         ----- this token may only be used once
7474 2 |     let _ = (token, token);
7475   |              -----  ^^^^^ value used here after move
7476   |              |
7477   |              value moved here
7478   |
7479   = note: you can create a new `Token` with `Token::conjure()`
7480```

7505    Lint {
7506        label: "diagnostic_on_unknown",
7507        description: r##"# `diagnostic_on_unknown`
7508
7509The tracking issue for this feature is: [#152900](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/152900)
7510
7511------------------------
7512
7513The `diagnostic_on_unknown` feature allows use of the `#[diagnostic::on_unknown]` attribute. It should be
7514placed on use and module declarations as well as the crate root, though it is not an error to be located in other
7515positions. This attribute is a hint to the compiler to supplement the error message when the
7516annotated declaration is involved in a name resolution error.
7517
7518Format parameters with the given named parameter will be replaced with the following text:
7519
7520-  `{Unresolved}` — The `SimplePathSegment` of the import path that could not be resolved.
7521-  `{this}` — The name of the annotated item. On `use` statements this is identical to `{unresolved}`.
7522
7523The original error message will not be suppressed but is emitted as a note instead.
7524
7525### On use declarations
7526
7527```rust,edition2018,compile_fail,E0432
7528#![feature(diagnostic_on_unknown)]
7529
7530#[diagnostic::on_unknown(
7531    message = "`{Unresolved}` doesn't exist",
7532    label = "you did something silly here"
7533)]
7534use doesnt_exist;
7535```
7536This will result in the following error:
7537```text
7538error[E0432]: `doesnt_exist` doesn't exist
7539 --> src/lib.rs:7:5
7540  |
75417 | use doesnt_exist;
7542  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^ you did something silly here
7543  |
7544  = note: unresolved import `doesnt_exist`
7545
7546For more information about this error, try `rustc --explain E0432`.
7547```
7548
7549### On module declarations
7550
7551```rust,edition2018,compile_fail,E0432
7552#![feature(diagnostic_on_unknown)]
7553
7554#[diagnostic::on_unknown(
7555    message = "module `{this}` is empty, there is no `{unresolved}` here",
7556    label = "can't import something from an empty module"
7557)]
7558mod empty {}
7559
7560use empty::what;
7561```
7562This will result in the following error:
7563
7564```text
7565error[E0432]: module `empty` is empty, there is no `what` here
7566 --> src/lib.rs:9:5
7567  |
75689 | use empty::what;
7569  |     ^^^^^^^----
7570  |            |
7571  |            can't import something from an empty module
7572  |
7573  = note: unresolved import `empty::what`
7574```
7575
7576### On the crate root
7577
7578This additionally requires the `#![feature(custom_inner_attributes)]` feature:
7579
7580```rust,edition2018,compile_fail,E0432
7581#![feature(diagnostic_on_unknown)]
7582#![feature(custom_inner_attributes)]
7583#![diagnostic::on_unknown(message = "Say `{Unresolved}` again!")]
7584
7585use self::what;
7586```
7587### Example
7588
7589Consider the following pair of macros, one which creates a hidden module with a constant and another that reads it.
7590
7591```rust
7592#![feature(macro_metavar_expr, macro_attr)]
7593
7594macro_rules! instrument {
7595    attr() { $vis:vis fn $fn_name:ident ($($arg_name:ident : $arg_ty:ty),*) $(-> $ret:ty)? $body:block } => {
7596        $vis fn $fn_name ($($arg_name:$arg_ty),*) $(-> $ret)? $body
7597        #[doc(hidden)]
7598        $vis mod $fn_name {
7599            pub const LEN: usize = ${ count($arg_name) };
7600        }
7601    }
7602}
7603
7604macro_rules! count_args {
7605    ($name:ident) => {{
7606        $name::LEN
7607    }}
7608}
7609
7610#[instrument]
7611fn add(a: u8, b: u8) -> u8 {
7612    a + b
7613}
7614
7615fn main() {
7616    let n = count_args!(add);
7617    println!("`add` has {n} arguments");
7618}
7619```
7620
7621If the `#[instrument]` macro is omitted it will emit this confusing error:
7622```text
7623error[E0433]: cannot find module or crate `add` in this scope
7624  --> src/main.rs:25:25
7625   |
762625 |     let n = count_args!(add);
7627   |                         ^^^ function `add` is not a crate or module
7628```
7629
7630`#[diagnostic::on_unknown]` can be used to customize this error message:
7631
7632```rust,edition2018,compile_fail,E0432
7633#![feature(diagnostic_on_unknown)]
7634# #![feature(macro_metavar_expr, macro_attr)]
7635#
7636# #[allow(unused_macros)]
7637# macro_rules! instrument {
7638#     attr() { $vis:vis fn $fn_name:ident ($($arg_name:ident : $arg_ty:ty),*) $(-> $ret:ty)? $body:block } => {
7639#         $vis fn $fn_name ($($arg_name:$arg_ty),*) $(-> $ret)? $body
7640#         #[doc(hidden)]
7641#         $vis  mod $fn_name {
7642#             pub const LEN: usize = ${ count($arg_name) };
7643#         }
7644#     }
7645# }
7646
7647macro_rules! count_args {
7648    ($name:ident) => {{
7649        #[diagnostic::on_unknown(
7650            message = "cannot count arguments of `{Unresolved}`",
7651            label = "`{Unresolved}` is not a function decorated \
7652                    with the `#[instrument]` macro"
7653        )]
7654        use $name::LEN as length;
7655        length
7656    }}
7657}
7658
7659// #[instrument]
7660fn add(a: u8, b: u8) -> u8 {
7661  a + b
7662}
7663
7664fn main() {
7665    let n = count_args!(add);
7666    println!("`add` has {n} arguments");
7667}
7668```
7669This produces:
7670```text
7671error[E0432]: cannot count arguments of `add`
7672  --> src/main.rs:33:25
7673   |
767433 |     let n = count_args!(add);
7675   |                         ^^^ `add` is not a function decorated with
7676   |                              the `#[instrument]` macro
7677   |
7678   = note: unresolved import `add`
7679```
7680
7681### Edition differences
7682
7683In the 2015 edition, use paths are relative to the crate root. For example, `use empty` will be resolved relative to the crate root and resolution will not encounter the `mod empty {}` declaration.
7684```rust,edition2015,compile_fail,E0432
7685#![feature(diagnostic_on_unknown)]
7686
7687mod foo {
7688   #[diagnostic::on_unknown(message = "oh oh")]
7689   mod empty {}
7690
7691   use empty::what;
7692}
7693```
7694
7695```text
7696error[E0432]: unresolved import `empty`
7697 --> src/main.rs:9:8
7698  |
76999 |    use empty::what;
7700  |        ^^^^^
7701  |
7702```

7715
7716------------------------
7717
7718The `diagnostic_on_unmatched_args` feature adds the
7719`#[diagnostic::on_unmatched_args(...)]` attribute for declarative macros.
7720It lets a macro definition customize diagnostics for matcher failures after all arms have been
7721tried, such as incomplete invocations or trailing extra arguments.
7722
7723This attribute currently applies to declarative macros such as `macro_rules!` and `pub macro`.
7724It is currently used for errors emitted by declarative macro matching itself; fragment parser
7725errors still use their existing diagnostics.
7726
7727```rust,compile_fail
7728#![feature(diagnostic_on_unmatched_args)]
7729
7730#[diagnostic::on_unmatched_args(
7731    message = "invalid arguments to {this} macro invocation",
7732    label = "expected a type and value here",
7733    note = "this macro expects a type and a value, like `pair!(u8, 0)`",
7734    note = "see <link/to/docs>",
7735)]
7736macro_rules! pair {
7737    ($ty:ty, $value:expr) => {};
7738}
7739
7740pair!(u8);
7741```
7742
7743This emits output like:
7744
7745```text
7746error: invalid arguments to pair macro invocation
7747  --> example.rs:13:9
7748   |
77499  | macro_rules! pair {
7750   | ----------------- when calling this macro
7751...
775213 | pair!(u8);
7753   |         ^ expected a type and value here
7754   |
7755note: while trying to match `,`
7756  --> example.rs:10:12
7757   |
775810 |     ($ty:ty, $value:expr) => {};
7759   |            ^
7760   = note: this macro expects a type and a value, like `pair!(u8, 0)`
7761   = note: see <link/to/docs>
7762```

7882------
7883
7884The `doc_cfg` feature allows an API be documented as only available in some specific platforms.
7885This attribute has two effects:
7886
78871. In the annotated item's documentation, there will be a message saying "Available on
7888    (platform) only".
7889
78902. The item's doc-tests will only run on the specific platform.
7891
7892In addition to allowing the use of the `#[doc(cfg)]` attribute, this feature enables the use of a
7893special conditional compilation flag, `#[cfg(doc)]`, set whenever building documentation on your
7894crate.
7895
7896This feature was introduced as part of PR [#43348] to allow the platform-specific parts of the
7897standard library be documented.
7898
7899```rust
7900#![feature(doc_cfg)]
7901
7902#[cfg(any(windows, doc))]
7903#[doc(cfg(windows))]
7904/// The application's icon in the notification area (a.k.a. system tray).
7905///
7906/// # Examples
7907///
7908/// ```no_run
7909/// extern crate my_awesome_ui_library;
7910/// use my_awesome_ui_library::current_app;
7911/// use my_awesome_ui_library::windows::notification;
7912///
7913/// let icon = current_app().get::<notification::Icon>();
7914/// icon.show();
7915/// icon.show_message("Hello");
7916/// ```
7917pub struct Icon {
7918    // ...
7919}
7920```
7921
7922[#43781]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/43781
7923[#43348]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/43348
7924"##,

7930        label: "doc_masked",
7931        description: r##"# `doc_masked`
7932
7933The tracking issue for this feature is: [#44027]

7935-----
7936
7937The `doc_masked` feature allows a crate to exclude types from a given crate from appearing in lists
7938of trait implementations. The specifics of the feature are as follows:
7939
79401. When rustdoc encounters an `extern crate` statement annotated with a `#[doc(masked)]` attribute,
7941   it marks the crate as being masked.
7942
79432. When listing traits a given type implements, rustdoc ensures that traits from masked crates are
7944   not emitted into the documentation.
7945
79463. When listing types that implement a given trait, rustdoc ensures that types from masked crates
7947   are not emitted into the documentation.
7948
7949This feature was introduced in PR [#44026] to ensure that compiler-internal and
7950implementation-specific types and traits were not included in the standard library's documentation.
7951Such types would introduce broken links into the documentation.
7952
7953[#44026]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/44026
7954[#44027]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/pull/44027
7955"##,
7956        default_severity: Severity::Allow,
7957        warn_since: None,
7958        deny_since: None,
7959    },
7960    Lint {
7961        label: "doc_notable_trait",
7962        description: r##"# `doc_notable_trait`
7963
7964The tracking issue for this feature is: [#45040]
7965
7966The `doc_notable_trait` feature allows the use of the `#[doc(notable_trait)]`
7967attribute, which will display the trait in a "Notable traits" dialog for
7968functions returning types that implement the trait. For example, this attribute
7969is applied to the `Iterator`, `Future`, `io::Read`, and `io::Write` traits in
7970the standard library.
7971
7972You can do this on your own traits like so:
7973
7974```
7975#![feature(doc_notable_trait)]
7976
7977#[doc(notable_trait)]
7978pub trait MyTrait {}
7979
7980pub struct MyStruct;
7981impl MyTrait for MyStruct {}
7982
7983/// The docs for this function will have a button that displays a dialog about
7984/// `MyStruct` implementing `MyTrait`.
7985pub fn my_fn() -> MyStruct { MyStruct }
7986```
7987
7988This feature was originally implemented in PR [#45039].
7989
7990See also its documentation in [the rustdoc book][rustdoc-book-notable_trait].

8411
8412The tracking issue for this feature is: [#134986]
8413
8414------
8415
8416Disallow `extern` without an explicit ABI. We should write `extern "C"`
8417(or another ABI) instead of just `extern`.
8418
8419By making the ABI explicit, it becomes much clearer that "C" is just one of the
8420possible choices, rather than the "standard" way for external functions.
8421Removing the default makes it easier to add a new ABI on equal footing as "C".
8422
8423```rust,editionfuture,compile_fail
8424#![feature(explicit_extern_abis)]
8425
8426extern fn function1() {}  // ERROR `extern` declarations without an explicit ABI
8427                          // are disallowed
8428
8429extern "C" fn function2() {} // compiles
8430
8431extern "aapcs" fn function3() {} // compiles
8432```
8433
8434[#134986]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/134986

8645        label: "ffi_const",
8646        description: r##"# `ffi_const`
8647
8648The tracking issue for this feature is: [#58328]
8649
8650------
8651
8652The `#[ffi_const]` attribute applies clang's `const` attribute to foreign
8653functions declarations.
8654
8655That is, `#[ffi_const]` functions shall have no effects except for its return
8656value, which can only depend on the values of the function parameters, and is
8657not affected by changes to the observable state of the program.
8658
8659Applying the `#[ffi_const]` attribute to a function that violates these
8660requirements is undefined behaviour.
8661
8662This attribute enables Rust to perform common optimizations, like sub-expression
8663elimination, and it can avoid emitting some calls in repeated invocations of the
8664function with the same argument values regardless of other operations being
8665performed in between these functions calls (as opposed to `#[ffi_pure]`
8666functions).
8667
8668## Pitfalls
8669
8670A `#[ffi_const]` function can only read global memory that would not affect
8671its return value for the whole execution of the program (e.g. immutable global
8672memory). `#[ffi_const]` functions are referentially-transparent and therefore
8673more strict than `#[ffi_pure]` functions.
8674
8675A common pitfall involves applying the `#[ffi_const]` attribute to a
8676function that reads memory through pointer arguments which do not necessarily
8677point to immutable global memory.
8678
8679A `#[ffi_const]` function that returns unit has no effect on the abstract
8680machine's state, and a `#[ffi_const]` function cannot be `#[ffi_pure]`.
8681
8682A `#[ffi_const]` function must not diverge, neither via a side effect (e.g. a
8683call to `abort`) nor by infinite loops.
8684
8685When translating C headers to Rust FFI, it is worth verifying for which targets
8686the `const` attribute is enabled in those headers, and using the appropriate
8687`cfg` macros in the Rust side to match those definitions. While the semantics of
8688`const` are implemented identically by many C and C++ compilers, e.g., clang,
8689[GCC], [ARM C/C++ compiler], [IBM ILE C/C++], etc. they are not necessarily
8690implemented in this way on all of them. It is therefore also worth verifying
8691that the semantics of the C toolchain used to compile the binary being linked
8692against are compatible with those of the `#[ffi_const]`.
8693
8694[#58328]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/58328
8695[ARM C/C++ compiler]: http://infocenter.arm.com/help/index.jsp?topic=/com.arm.doc.dui0491c/Cacgigch.html
8696[GCC]: https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Common-Function-Attributes.html#index-const-function-attribute
8697[IBM ILE C/C++]: https://www.ibm.com/support/knowledgecenter/fr/ssw_ibm_i_71/rzarg/fn_attrib_const.htm
8698"##,
8699        default_severity: Severity::Allow,

8701        deny_since: None,
8702    },
8703    Lint {
8704        label: "ffi_pure",
8705        description: r##"# `ffi_pure`
8706
8707The tracking issue for this feature is: [#58329]
8708
8709------
8710
8711The `#[ffi_pure]` attribute applies clang's `pure` attribute to foreign
8712functions declarations.
8713
8714That is, `#[ffi_pure]` functions shall have no effects except for its return
8715value, which shall not change across two consecutive function calls with
8716the same parameters.
8717
8718Applying the `#[ffi_pure]` attribute to a function that violates these
8719requirements is undefined behavior.
8720
8721This attribute enables Rust to perform common optimizations, like sub-expression
8722elimination and loop optimizations. Some common examples of pure functions are
8723`strlen` or `memcmp`.
8724
8725These optimizations are only applicable when the compiler can prove that no
8726program state observable by the `#[ffi_pure]` function has changed between calls
8727of the function, which could alter the result. See also the `#[ffi_const]`
8728attribute, which provides stronger guarantees regarding the allowable behavior
8729of a function, enabling further optimization.
8730
8731## Pitfalls
8732
8733A `#[ffi_pure]` function can read global memory through the function
8734parameters (e.g. pointers), globals, etc. `#[ffi_pure]` functions are not
8735referentially-transparent, and are therefore more relaxed than `#[ffi_const]`
8736functions.
8737
8738However, accessing global memory through volatile or atomic reads can violate the
8739requirement that two consecutive function calls shall return the same value.
8740
8741A `pure` function that returns unit has no effect on the abstract machine's
8742state.
8743
8744A `#[ffi_pure]` function must not diverge, neither via a side effect (e.g. a
8745call to `abort`) nor by infinite loops.
8746
8747When translating C headers to Rust FFI, it is worth verifying for which targets
8748the `pure` attribute is enabled in those headers, and using the appropriate
8749`cfg` macros in the Rust side to match those definitions. While the semantics of
8750`pure` are implemented identically by many C and C++ compilers, e.g., clang,
8751[GCC], [ARM C/C++ compiler], [IBM ILE C/C++], etc. they are not necessarily
8752implemented in this way on all of them. It is therefore also worth verifying
8753that the semantics of the C toolchain used to compile the binary being linked
8754against are compatible with those of the `#[ffi_pure]`.
8755
8756
8757[#58329]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/58329
8758[ARM C/C++ compiler]: http://infocenter.arm.com/help/index.jsp?topic=/com.arm.doc.dui0491c/Cacigdac.html
8759[GCC]: https://gcc.gnu.org/onlinedocs/gcc/Common-Function-Attributes.html#index-pure-function-attribute
8760[IBM ILE C/C++]: https://www.ibm.com/support/knowledgecenter/fr/ssw_ibm_i_71/rzarg/fn_attrib_pure.htm

9116----
9117
9118The `fn_traits` feature allows for implementation of the [`Fn*`] traits
9119for creating custom closure-like types.
9120
9121[`Fn*`]: ../../std/ops/trait.Fn.html
9122
9123```rust
9124#![feature(unboxed_closures)]
9125#![feature(fn_traits)]
9126
9127struct Adder {
9128    a: u32
9129}
9130
9131impl FnOnce<(u32, )> for Adder {
9132    type Output = u32;
9133    extern "rust-call" fn call_once(self, b: (u32, )) -> Self::Output {
9134        self.a + b.0
9135    }
9136}
9137
9138fn main() {
9139    let adder = Adder { a: 3 };
9140    assert_eq!(adder(2), 5);
9141}
9142```

9263
9264The `frontmatter` feature allows an extra metadata block at the top of files for consumption by
9265external tools. For example, it can be used by [`cargo-script`] files to specify dependencies.
9266
9267```rust
9268#!/usr/bin/env -S cargo -Zscript
9269---
9270[dependencies]
9271libc = "0.2.172"
9272---
9273#![feature(frontmatter)]
9274# mod libc { pub type c_int = i32; }
9275
9276fn main() {
9277    let x: libc::c_int = 1i32;
9278}
9279```

9328------------------------
9329
9330The `#![feature(function_arg_const_generics)]` allows const generic parameters to be declared in a function's value parameter list and supplied as ordinary call arguments, rather than through generic arguments (turbofish syntax).
9331
9332Warning: This feature is incomplete; its design and syntax may change.
9333
9334This feature requires either `#![feature(gca_min_const_items)]` or `#![feature(gca_adts)]`.
9335
9336## Examples
9337
9338Normally, const generic parameters are declared in the generic parameter list and supplied using turbofish syntax:
9339
9340```rust
9341fn foo<const N: usize>(value: u8) {
9342    let _ = N;
9343}
9344
9345fn main() {
9346    foo::<42>(10);
9347}
9348```
9349
9350With `function_arg_const_generics`, the const generic parameter can instead be declared in the function's value parameter list:
9351
9352```rust
9353#![allow(incomplete_features)]
9354#![feature(function_arg_const_generics, gca_min_const_items)]
9355
9356fn foo(const N: usize, value: u8) {
9357    let _ = (N, value);
9358}
9359
9360fn main() {
9361    foo(42, 10);
9362}
9363```
9364
9365Here, `N` is still a const generic parameter, but its value is supplied as the first argument to the function call.
9366
9367### Methods and trait functions
9368
9369Argument position const generic parameters are supported in free functions, inherent methods, trait methods, and trait implementations.
9370
9371```rust
9372#![allow(incomplete_features)]
9373#![feature(function_arg_const_generics, gca_min_const_items)]
9374
9375struct Foo;
9376
9377impl Foo {
9378    fn bar(&self, const N: usize) {
9379        let _ = N;
9380    }
9381}
9382
9383trait Trait {
9384    fn baz(const N: usize);
9385}
9386
9387impl Trait for Foo {
9388    fn baz(const N: usize) {
9389        let _ = N;
9390    }
9391}
9392
9393fn main() {
9394    Foo.bar(10);
9395    Foo::baz(20);
9396}
9397```
9398
9399### Supported const arguments
9400
9401Currently, only the following forms of const arguments are supported:
9402
9403- Literals.
9404- Paths to const generic parameters.
9405- Paths to const items, provided the const item is marked for use in the type system, for example using `gca!`.
9406
9407```rust
9408#![allow(incomplete_features)]
9409#![feature(function_arg_const_generics, gca_min_const_items)]
9410
9411fn foo(const N: usize) {
9412    let _ = N;
9413}
9414
9415const VALUE: usize = core::gca!(42);
9416
9417fn bar<const K: usize>() {
9418    foo(K);
9419}
9420
9421fn main() {
9422    foo(10);    // OK: integer literal
9423    foo(VALUE); // OK: const item marked with gca!
9424    bar::<20>();
9425}
9426```
9427
9428### Restrictions
9429
9430Argument position const generic parameters have the following restrictions:
9431
9432- They must be declared using a plain identifier, such as `const N: usize`.
9433- They cannot be explicitly supplied using turbofish syntax.
9434- Arguments must use one of the supported const argument forms described above.
9435
9436For example, a runtime local variable cannot be used as a const argument:
9437
9438```rust,compile_fail
9439#![allow(incomplete_features)]
9440#![feature(function_arg_const_generics, gca_min_const_items)]
9441
9442fn foo(const N: usize) {}
9443
9444fn main() {
9445    let n = 10;
9446    foo(n); // ERROR: runtime local variable
9447}
9448```
9449
9450Similarly, argument position const generic parameters cannot be specified using turbofish syntax:
9451
9452```rust,compile_fail,E0107
9453#![allow(incomplete_features)]
9454#![feature(function_arg_const_generics, gca_min_const_items)]
9455
9456fn foo(const N: usize) {}
9457
9458fn main() {
9459    foo::<10>(10); // ERROR: N cannot be specified using turbofish
9460}
9461```
9462
9463Argument position const generic parameters are not currently supported in function pointer types, `Fn()` trait syntax, or foreign function declarations.

9597## Examples
9598
9599Here is an example from [gca_min_const_items]:
9600
9601[gca_min_const_items]: gca-min-const-items.md
9602
9603```rust
9604#![allow(incomplete_features)]
9605#![feature(gca_min_const_items)]
9606
9607trait Bar {
9608    #[rustc_always_gca]
9609    const VAL: usize;
9610    #[rustc_always_gca]
9611    const VAL2: usize;
9612}
9613
9614struct Baz;
9615
9616impl Bar for Baz {
9617    const VAL: usize = core::gca!(2);
9618    const VAL2: usize = core::gca!(const { Self::VAL * 2 });
9619}
9620
9621struct Foo<B: Bar> {
9622    arr1: [usize; core::gca!(B::VAL)],
9623    arr2: [usize; core::gca!(B::VAL2)],
9624}
9625```
9626
9627Using `#![feature(gca_macroless_args)]` enables you to write the above without the macro:
9628
9629```rust
9630#![allow(incomplete_features)]
9631#![feature(gca_min_const_items, gca_macroless_args)]
9632
9633trait Bar {
9634    #[rustc_always_gca]
9635    const VAL: usize;
9636    #[rustc_always_gca]
9637    const VAL2: usize;
9638}
9639
9640struct Baz;
9641
9642impl Bar for Baz {
9643    // note these still need a macro, macroless for these is `gca_macroless_items`
9644    const VAL: usize = core::gca!(2);
9645    const VAL2: usize = core::gca!(const { Self::VAL * 2 });
9646}
9647
9648struct Foo<B: Bar> {
9649    arr1: [usize; B::VAL],
9650    arr2: [usize; B::VAL2],
9651}
9652```

9695
9696trait Trait {
9697    const ASSOC<const N: usize>: usize;
9698}
9699
9700impl Trait for () {
9701    const ASSOC<const N: usize>: usize = core::gca!(N);
9702}
9703
9704fn foo<const N: usize>() {
9705    let a: [(); <() as Trait>::ASSOC::<N>]
9706        = [(); N];
9707}
9708```
9709
9710Using `#![feature(gca_macroless_items)]` enables you to write the above without the macro:
9711
9712```rust,ignore (needs new solver)
9713#![allow(incomplete_features)]
9714#![feature(
9715    gca_min_const_items,
9716    gca_const_items,
9717    gca_macroless_args,
9718    gca_macroless_items,
9719    generic_const_items,
9720)]
9721
9722trait Trait {
9723    const ASSOC<const N: usize>: usize;
9724}
9725
9726impl Trait for () {
9727    const ASSOC<const N: usize>: usize = N;
9728}
9729
9730fn foo<const N: usize>() {
9731    let a: [(); <() as Trait>::ASSOC::<N>]
9732        = [(); N];
9733}
9734```

9751
9752Warning: This feature is incomplete; its design and syntax may change.
9753
9754This feature acts as a minimal alternative to [generic_const_exprs] that allows a smaller subset of functionality,
9755and uses a different approach for implementation. It is intentionally more restrictive, which helps with avoiding edge
9756cases that make the `generic_const_exprs` hard to implement properly. See [Feature background][feature_background]
9757for more details.
9758
9759Related features: [gca_macroless_args], [gca_const_items], [generic_const_items].
9760
9761[feature_background]: https://github.com/rust-lang/project-const-generics/blob/main/documents/min_const_generics_plan.md
9762[generic_const_exprs]: generic-const-exprs.md
9763[gca_macroless_args]: gca-macroless-args.md
9764[gca_const_items]: gca-const-items.md
9765[generic_const_items]: generic-const-items.md
9766
9767## `gca!` macro
9768
9769This feature introduces a new macro: `gca!`.
9770
9771When an expression is used as a generic argument, it is typically lowered as an "anon const", which is an expression
9772that is opaque to the type system and cannot contain generics. Using `gca!` instead represents the
9773expression "directly", i.e. without an anon const, in a way that is visible to the type system.
9774
9775(Note that plain paths to generic parameters are always represented directly, without `gca!`, as this
9776already works on stable)
9777
9778See [gca_macroless_args] as a feature to disable the requirement of writing `gca!`.
9779
9780[gca_macroless_args]: gca-macroless-args.md
9781
9782## direct const items
9783
9784This feature introduces a new item kind: consts with a `gca!` right-hand side.
9785Constants with a direct right-hand side are allowed to be used in type contexts, e.g.:
9786
9787```compile_fail
9788#![allow(incomplete_features)]
9789#![feature(gca_min_const_items)]
9790
9791const X: usize = core::gca!(1);
9792const Y: usize = 1;
9793
9794struct Foo {
9795    good_arr: [(); core::gca!(X)], // Allowed
9796    bad_arr: [(); core::gca!(Y)], // Will not compile
9797}
9798```
9799
9800## Examples
9801
9802```rust
9803#![allow(incomplete_features)]
9804#![feature(gca_min_const_items)]
9805
9806trait Bar {
9807    #[rustc_always_gca]
9808    const VAL: usize;
9809    #[rustc_always_gca]
9810    const VAL2: usize;
9811}
9812
9813struct Baz;
9814
9815impl Bar for Baz {
9816    const VAL: usize = core::gca!(2);
9817    const VAL2: usize = core::gca!(const { Self::VAL * 2 });
9818}
9819
9820struct Foo<B: Bar> {
9821    arr1: [usize; core::gca!(B::VAL)],
9822    arr2: [usize; core::gca!(B::VAL2)],
9823}
9824```
9825
9826Note that with [generic_const_exprs] the same example would look as follows:
9827
9828```rust
9829#![allow(incomplete_features)]
9830#![feature(generic_const_exprs)]
9831
9832trait Bar {
9833    const VAL: usize;
9834    const VAL2: usize;
9835}
9836
9837struct Baz;
9838
9839impl Bar for Baz {
9840    const VAL: usize = 2;
9841    const VAL2: usize = const { Self::VAL * 2 };
9842}
9843
9844struct Foo<B: Bar>
9845where
9846    [(); B::VAL]:,
9847    [(); B::VAL2]:,
9848{
9849    arr1: [usize; B::VAL],
9850    arr2: [usize; B::VAL2],
9851}
9852```
9853
9854Use of const functions is allowed:
9855
9856```rust
9857#![allow(incomplete_features)]
9858#![feature(gca_min_const_items)]
9859
9860const VAL: usize = 1;
9861
9862const fn inc(val: usize) -> usize {
9863    val + 1
9864}
9865
9866const INC: usize = core::gca!(const { inc(VAL) });
9867
9868const ARR: [usize; INC] = [0; INC];
9869```

9972## Examples
9973
9974```rust
9975#![allow(incomplete_features)]
9976#![feature(generic_const_exprs)]
9977
9978// Use parameters that depend on a generic argument.
9979struct Foo<const N: usize>
9980where
9981    [(); N + 1]:,
9982{
9983    array: [usize; N + 1],
9984}
9985
9986// Use generic parameters in const operations.
9987trait Bar {
9988    const X: usize;
9989    const Y: usize;
9990}
9991
9992// Note `B::X * B::Y`.
9993const fn baz<B: Bar>(x: [usize; B::X], y: [usize; B::Y]) -> [usize; B::X * B::Y] {
9994    let mut out = [0; B::X * B::Y];
9995    let mut i = 0;
9996    while i < B::Y {
9997        let mut j = 0;
9998        while j < B::X {
9999            out[i * B::X + j] = y[i].saturating_mul(x[j]);
10000            j += 1;
10001        }
10002        i += 1;
10003    }
10004    out
10005}
10006
10007
10008// Create a new type based on a generic argument.
10009pub struct Grow<const N: usize> {
10010    arr: [usize; N],
10011}
10012
10013impl<const N: usize> Grow<N> {
10014    pub const fn grow(self, val: usize) -> Grow<{ N + 1 }> {
10015        let mut new_arr = [0; { N + 1 }];
10016        let mut idx = 0;
10017        while idx < N {
10018            new_arr[idx] = self.arr[idx];
10019            idx += 1;
10020        }
10021        new_arr[N] = val;
10022        Grow { arr: new_arr }
10023    }
10024}
10025```

10052## Examples
10053
10054### Generic constant values
10055
10056```rust
10057#![allow(incomplete_features)]
10058#![feature(generic_const_items)]
10059
10060const GENERIC_VAL<const ARG: usize>: usize = ARG + 1;
10061
10062#[test]
10063fn generic_const_arg() {
10064    assert_eq!(GENERIC_VAL::<1>, 2);
10065    assert_eq!(GENERIC_VAL::<2>, 3);
10066}
10067```
10068
10069### Conditional constants
10070
10071```rust
10072#![allow(incomplete_features)]
10073#![feature(generic_const_items)]
10074
10075// `GENERIC_VAL::<0>` will fail to compile
10076const GENERIC_VAL<const ARG: usize>: usize = if ARG > 0 { ARG + 1 } else { panic!("0 value") };
10077
10078// Will fail to compile if the `Copy` derive is removed.
10079const COPY_MARKER<C: Copy>: () = ();
10080
10081#[derive(Clone, Copy)]
10082struct Foo;
10083
10084const FOO_IS_COPY: () = COPY_MARKER::<Foo>;
10085```

10255
10256This feature allow using top-level half-open range patterns in slices.
10257
10258```rust
10259#![feature(half_open_range_patterns_in_slices)]
10260
10261fn main() {
10262    let xs = [13, 1, 5, 2, 3, 1, 21, 8];
10263    let [a @ 3.., b @ ..3, c @ 4..6, ..] = xs else { return; };
10264}
10265```
10266
10267Note that this feature is not required if the patterns are wrapped between parenthesis.
10268
10269```rust
10270fn main() {
10271    let xs = [13, 1];
10272    let [(a @ 3..), c] = xs else { return; };
10273}
10274```

10488

10490}

10690        label: "intrinsics",
10691        description: r##"# `intrinsics`
