10698
10699------------------------
10700
10701
10702## Intrinsics with fallback logic
10703
10704Many intrinsics can be written in pure rust, albeit inefficiently or without supporting
10705some features that only exist on some backends. Backends can simply not implement those
10706intrinsics without causing any code miscompilations or failures to compile.
10707All intrinsic fallback bodies are automatically made cross-crate inlineable (like `#[inline]`)
10708by the codegen backend, but not the MIR inliner.
10709
10710```rust
10711#![feature(intrinsics)]
10712#![allow(internal_features)]
10713
10714#[rustc_intrinsic]
10715const unsafe fn const_deallocate(_ptr: *mut u8, _size: usize, _align: usize) {}
10716```
10717
10718Since these are just regular functions, it is perfectly ok to create the intrinsic twice:
10719
10720```rust
10721#![feature(intrinsics)]
10722#![allow(internal_features)]
10723
10724#[rustc_intrinsic]
10725const unsafe fn const_deallocate(_ptr: *mut u8, _size: usize, _align: usize) {}
10726
10727mod foo {
10728    #[rustc_intrinsic]
10729    const unsafe fn const_deallocate(_ptr: *mut u8, _size: usize, _align: usize) {
10730        panic!("noisy const dealloc")
10731    }
10732}
10733
10734```
10735
10736The behaviour on backends that override the intrinsic is exactly the same. On other
10737backends, the intrinsic behaviour depends on which implementation is called, just like
10738with any regular function.
10739
10740## Intrinsics lowered to MIR instructions
10741
10742Various intrinsics have native MIR operations that they correspond to. Instead of requiring
10743backends to implement both the intrinsic and the MIR operation, the `lower_intrinsics` pass
10744will convert the calls to the MIR operation. Backends do not need to know about these intrinsics
10745at all. These intrinsics only make sense without a body, and can be declared as a `#[rustc_intrinsic]`.
10746The body is never used as the lowering pass implements support for all backends, so we never have to
10747use the fallback logic.
10748
10749## Intrinsics without fallback logic
10750
10751These must be implemented by all backends.
10752
10753### `#[rustc_intrinsic]` declarations
10754
10755These are written without a body:
10756```rust
10757#![feature(intrinsics)]
10758#![allow(internal_features)]
10759
10760#[rustc_intrinsic]
10761pub fn abort_immediate() -> !;
10762```

11248The `rustc` compiler has certain pluggable operations, that is,
11249functionality that isn't hard-coded into the language, but is
11250implemented in libraries, with a special marker to tell the compiler
11251it exists. The marker is the attribute `#[lang = "..."]` and there are
11252various different values of `...`, i.e. various different 'lang
11253items'. Most of them can only be defined once.
11254
11255Lang items are loaded lazily by the compiler; e.g. if one never uses `Box`
11256then there is no need to define a function for `exchange_malloc`.
11257`rustc` will emit an error when an item is needed but not found in the current
11258crate or any that it depends on.
11259
11260Some features provided by lang items:
11261
11262- overloadable operators via traits: the traits corresponding to the
11263  `==`, `<`, dereferencing (`*`) and `+` (etc.) operators are all
11264  marked with lang items; those specific four are `eq`, `partial_ord`,
11265  `deref`/`deref_mut`, and `add` respectively.
11266- panicking: the `panic` and `panic_impl` lang items, among others.
11267- stack unwinding: the lang item `eh_personality` is a function used by the
11268  failure mechanisms of the compiler. This is often mapped to GCC's personality
11269  function (see the [`std` implementation][personality] for more information),
11270  but programs which don't trigger a panic can be assured that this function is
11271  never called.
11272- the traits in `core::marker` used to indicate types of
11273  various kinds; e.g. lang items `sized`, `sync` and `copy`.
11274- memory allocation, see below.
11275
11276Most lang items are defined by `core`, but if you're trying to build
11277an executable without the `std` crate, you might run into the need
11278for lang item definitions.
11279
11280[personality]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/HEAD/library/std/src/sys/personality/gcc.rs
11281
11282## Example: Implementing a `Box`
11283
11284`Box` pointers require two lang items: one for the type itself and one for
11285allocation. A freestanding program that uses the `Box` sugar for dynamic
11286allocations via `malloc` and `free`:
11287
11288```rust,ignore (libc-is-finicky)
11289#![feature(lang_items, core_intrinsics, rustc_private, panic_unwind, rustc_attrs)]
11290#![allow(internal_features)]
11291#![no_std]
11292#![no_main]
11293
11294extern crate libc;
11295extern crate unwind;
11296
11297use core::ffi::{c_int, c_void};
11298use core::intrinsics;
11299use core::panic::PanicInfo;
11300use core::ptr::NonNull;
11301
11302pub struct Global; // the global allocator
11303struct Unique<T>(NonNull<T>);
11304
11305#[lang = "owned_box"]
11306pub struct Box<T, A = Global>(Unique<T>, A);
11307
11308impl<T> Box<T> {
11309    pub fn new(x: T) -> Self {
11310        #[rustc_box]
11311        Box::new(x)
11312    }
11313}
11314
11315impl<T, A> Drop for Box<T, A> {
11316    fn drop(&mut self) {
11317        unsafe {
11318            libc::free(self.0.0.as_ptr() as *mut c_void);
11319        }
11320    }
11321}
11322
11323#[lang = "exchange_malloc"]
11324unsafe fn allocate(size: usize, _align: usize) -> *mut u8 {
11325    let p = libc::malloc(size) as *mut u8;
11326
11327    // Check if `malloc` failed:
11328    if p.is_null() {
11329        intrinsics::abort_immediate();
11330    }
11331
11332    p
11333}
11334
11335#[no_mangle]
11336extern "C" fn main(_argc: c_int, _argv: *const *const u8) -> c_int {
11337    let _x = Box::new(1);
11338
11339    0
11340}
11341
11342#[lang = "eh_personality"]
11343fn rust_eh_personality() {}
11344
11345#[panic_handler]
11346fn panic_handler(_info: &PanicInfo) -> ! { intrinsics::abort_immediate() }
11347```
11348
11349Note the use of `abort`: the `exchange_malloc` lang item is assumed to
11350return a valid pointer, and so needs to do the check internally.
11351

11458The `link_arg_attribute` feature allows passing arguments into the linker
11459from inside of the source code. Order is preserved for link attributes as
11460they were defined on a single extern block:
11461
11462```rust,no_run
11463#![feature(link_arg_attribute)]
11464
11465#[link(kind = "link-arg", name = "--start-group")]
11466#[link(kind = "static", name = "c")]
11467#[link(kind = "static", name = "gcc")]
11468#[link(kind = "link-arg", name = "--end-group")]
11469extern "C" {}
11470```

11672------
11673
11674<!--
11675FIXME(#159429): temporarily renamed `#[unroll]` to mitigate a nameres ambiguity
11676-->
11677
11678Loop unrolling can be a powerful optimization but like inlining, it is sometimes useful to
11679manually provide hints to optimizations.
11680
11681`#[rustc_unroll]` will encourage unrolling of a loop.
11682
11683`#[rustc_unroll(full)]` is a stronger hint and can cause optimizations to completely ignore the code
11684side growth from repeating a loop body.
11685
11686`#[rustc_unroll(never)]` is a strong hint to not unroll the loop at all. Note that other loop
11687optimizations may still be applied.
11688
11689`#[rustc_unroll(N)]` is a hint to unroll `N` iterations of the loop.
11690
11691In all cases these are just hints and may be ignored. But unlike function inlining hints,
11692loops tend to be heavily modified during compilation, which can make obeying hints challenging.
11693If the attribute doesn't do what you want, please file an issue.
11694"##,
11695        default_severity: Severity::Allow,
11696        warn_since: None,
11697        deny_since: None,
11698    },
11699    Lint {
11700        label: "loop_match",
11701        description: r##"# `loop_match`
11702
11703The tracking issue for this feature is: [#132306]
11704
11705[#132306]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/132306

11707------
11708
11709The `#[loop_match]` and `#[const_continue]` attributes can be used to improve the code
11710generation of logic that fits this shape:
11711
11712```ignore (pseudo-rust)
11713loop {
11714    state = 'blk: {
11715        match state {
11716            State::A => {
11717                break 'blk State::B
11718            }
11719            State::B => { /* ... */ }
11720            /* ... */
11721        }
11722    }
11723}
11724```
11725
11726Here the loop itself can be annotated with `#[loop_match]`, and any `break 'blk` with
11727`#[const_continue]` if the value is know at compile time:
11728
11729```ignore (pseudo-rust)
11730#[loop_match]
11731loop {
11732    state = 'blk: {
11733        match state {
11734            State::A => {
11735                #[const_continue]
11736                break 'blk State::B
11737            }
11738            State::B => { /* ... */ }
11739            /* ... */
11740        }
11741    }
11742}
11743```
11744
11745The observable behavior of this loop is exactly the same as without the extra attributes.
11746The difference is in the generated output: normally, when the state is `A`, control flow
11747moves from the `A` branch, back to the top of the loop, then to the `B` branch. With the
11748attributes, The `A` branch will immediately jump to the `B` branch.
11749
11750Removing the indirection can be beneficial for stack usage and branch prediction, and
11751enables other optimizations by clearly splitting out the control flow paths that your
11752program will actually use.

11845------------------------
11846
11847In stable Rust, there is no way to create new identifiers by joining identifiers to literals or other identifiers without using procedural macros such as [`paste`].
11848 `#![feature(macro_metavar_expr_concat)]` introduces a way to do this, using the concat metavariable expression.
11849
11850> This feature uses the syntax from [`macro_metavar_expr`] but is otherwise
11851> independent. It replaces the since-removed unstable feature
11852> [`concat_idents`].
11853
11854> This is an experimental feature; it and its syntax will require a RFC before stabilization.
11855
11856
11857### Overview
11858
11859`#![feature(macro_metavar_expr_concat)]` provides the `concat` metavariable expression for creating new identifiers:
11860
11861```rust
11862#![feature(macro_metavar_expr_concat)]
11863
11864macro_rules! create_some_structs {
11865    ($name:ident) => {
11866        pub struct ${ concat(First, $name) };
11867        pub struct ${ concat(Second, $name) };
11868        pub struct ${ concat(Third, $name) };
11869    }
11870}
11871
11872create_some_structs!(Thing);
11873```
11874
11875This macro invocation expands to:
11876
11877```rust
11878pub struct FirstThing;
11879pub struct SecondThing;
11880pub struct ThirdThing;
11881```
11882
11883### Syntax
11884
11885This feature builds upon the metavariable expression syntax `${ .. }` as specified in [RFC 3086] ([`macro_metavar_expr`]).
11886 `concat` is available like `${ concat(items) }`, where `items` is a comma separated sequence of idents and/or literals.
11887
11888### Examples
11889
11890#### Create a function or method with a concatenated name
11891
11892```rust
11893#![feature(macro_metavar_expr_concat)]
11894
11895macro_rules! make_getter {
11896    ($name:ident, $field: ident, $ret:ty) => {
11897        impl $name {
11898            pub fn ${ concat(get_, $field) }(&self) -> &$ret {
11899                &self.$field
11900            }
11901        }
11902    }
11903}
11904
11905pub struct Thing {
11906    description: String,
11907}
11908
11909make_getter!(Thing, description, String);
11910```
11911
11912This expands to:
11913
11914```rust
11915pub struct Thing {
11916    description: String,
11917}
11918
11919impl Thing {
11920    pub fn get_description(&self) -> &String {
11921        &self.description
11922    }
11923}
11924```
11925
11926#### Create names for macro generated tests
11927
11928```rust
11929#![feature(macro_metavar_expr_concat)]
11930
11931macro_rules! test_math {
11932    ($integer:ident) => {
11933        #[test]
11934        fn ${ concat(test_, $integer, _, addition) } () {
11935            let a: $integer = 73;
11936            let b: $integer = 42;
11937            assert_eq!(a + b, 115)
11938        }
11939
11940        #[test]
11941        fn ${ concat(test_, $integer, _, subtraction) } () {
11942            let a: $integer = 73;
11943            let b: $integer = 42;
11944            assert_eq!(a - b, 31)
11945        }
11946    }
11947}
11948
11949test_math!(i32);
11950test_math!(u64);
11951test_math!(u128);
11952```
11953
11954Running this returns the following output:
11955
11956```text
11957running 6 tests
11958test test_i32_subtraction ... ok
11959test test_i32_addition ... ok
11960test test_u128_addition ... ok
11961test test_u128_subtraction ... ok
11962test test_u64_addition ... ok
11963test test_u64_subtraction ... ok
11964
11965test result: ok. 6 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 0 measured; 0 filtered out; finished in 0.00s
11966```

12030
12031The tracking issue for this feature is: [#29864]
12032
12033[#29864]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/29864
12034
12035------------------------
12036
12037Normally, Rust keeps you from adding trait implementations that could
12038overlap with each other, as it would be ambiguous which to use.  This
12039feature, however, carves out an exception to that rule: a trait can
12040opt-in to having overlapping implementations, at the cost that those
12041implementations are not allowed to override anything (and thus the
12042trait itself cannot have any associated items, as they're pointless
12043when they'd need to do the same thing for every type anyway).
12044
12045```rust
12046#![feature(marker_trait_attr)]
12047
12048#[marker] trait CheapToClone: Clone {}
12049
12050impl<T: Copy> CheapToClone for T {}
12051
12052// These could potentially overlap with the blanket implementation above,
12053// so are only allowed because CheapToClone is a marker trait.
12054impl<T: CheapToClone, U: CheapToClone> CheapToClone for (T, U) {}
12055impl<T: CheapToClone> CheapToClone for std::ops::Range<T> {}
12056
12057fn cheap_clone<T: CheapToClone>(t: T) -> T {
12058    t.clone()
12059}
12060```
12061
12062This is expected to replace the unstable `overlapping_marker_traits`
12063feature, which applied to all empty traits (without needing an opt-in).

12270## Example
12271
12272```rust
12273#![feature(more_qualified_paths)]
12274

12278}

12280struct StructStruct {
12281    br: i8,
12282}
12283
12284struct Foo;
12285
12286trait A {
12287    type Assoc;
12288}
12289
12290impl A for Foo {
12291    type Assoc = StructStruct;
12292}

12563------------------------
12564
12565The `native_link_modifiers_as_needed` feature allows you to use the `as-needed` modifier.
12566
12567`as-needed` is only compatible with the `dynamic` and `framework` linking kinds. Using any other kind will result in a compiler error.
12568
12569`+as-needed` means that the library will be actually linked only if it satisfies some undefined symbols at the point at which it is specified on the command line, making it similar to static libraries in this regard.
12570
12571This modifier translates to `--as-needed` for ld-like linkers, and to `-dead_strip_dylibs` / `-needed_library` / `-needed_framework` for ld64.
12572The modifier does nothing for linkers that don't support it (e.g. `link.exe`).
12573
12574The default for this modifier is unclear, some targets currently specify it as `+as-needed`, some do not. We may want to try making `+as-needed` a default for all targets.

12611        label: "negative_impls",
12612        description: r##"# `negative_impls`
12613
12614The tracking issue for this feature is [#68318].
12615
12616[#68318]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/68318
12617
12618----
12619
12620With the feature gate `negative_impls`, you can write negative impls as well as positive ones:
12621
12622```rust
12623#![feature(negative_impls)]
12624trait DerefMut { }
12625impl<T: ?Sized> !DerefMut for &T { }
12626```
12627
12628Negative impls indicate a semver guarantee that the given trait will not be implemented for the given types. Negative impls play an additional purpose for auto traits, described below.
12629
12630Negative impls have the following characteristics:
12631
12632* They do not have any items.
12633* They must obey the orphan rules as if they were a positive impl.
12634* They cannot "overlap" with any positive impls.
12635
12636## Semver interaction
12637
12638It is a breaking change to remove a negative impl. Negative impls are a commitment not to implement the given trait for the named types.
12639
12640## Orphan and overlap rules
12641
12642Negative impls must obey the same orphan rules as a positive impl. This implies you cannot add a negative impl for types defined in upstream crates and so forth.
12643
12644Similarly, negative impls cannot overlap with positive impls, again using the same "overlap" check that we ordinarily use to determine if two impls overlap. (Note that positive impls typically cannot overlap with one another either, except as permitted by specialization.)
12645
12646## Interaction with auto traits
12647
12648Declaring a negative impl `impl !SomeAutoTrait for SomeType` for an
12649auto-trait serves two purposes:
12650
12651* as with any trait, it declares that `SomeType` will never implement `SomeAutoTrait`;
12652* it disables the automatic `SomeType: SomeAutoTrait` impl that would otherwise have been generated.
12653
12654Note that, at present, there is no way to indicate that a given type
12655does not implement an auto trait *but that it may do so in the
12656future*. For ordinary types, this is done by simply not declaring any
12657impl at all, but that is not an option for auto traits. A workaround
12658is that one could embed a marker type as one of the fields, where the
12659marker type is `!AutoTrait`.
12660
12661## Immediate uses
12662
12663Negative impls are used to declare that `&T: !DerefMut`  and `&mut T: !Clone`, as required to fix the soundness of `Pin` described in [#66544](https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/66544).
12664
12665This serves two purposes:
12666
12667* For proving the correctness of unsafe code, we can use that impl as evidence that no `DerefMut` or `Clone` impl exists.
12668* It prevents downstream crates from creating such impls.

13003
13004The tracking issue for this feature is: [#120141]
13005
13006[#120141]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/120141
13007
13008------------------------
13009
13010When the `offset_of_enum` feature is enabled, the [`offset_of!`] macro may be used to obtain the
13011offsets of fields of `enum`s; to express this, `enum` variants may be traversed as if they were
13012fields. Variants themselves do not have an offset, so they cannot appear as the last path component.
13013
13014```rust
13015#![feature(offset_of_enum)]
13016use std::mem;
13017
13018#[repr(u8)]
13019enum Enum {
13020    A(u8, u16),
13021    B { one: u8, two: u16 },
13022}
13023
13024assert_eq!(mem::offset_of!(Enum, A.0), 1);
13025assert_eq!(mem::offset_of!(Enum, B.two), 2);
13026
13027assert_eq!(mem::offset_of!(Option<&u8>, Some.0), 0);
13028```
13029
13030[`offset_of!`]: ../../std/mem/macro.offset_of.html
13031"##,

13039
13040The tracking issue for this feature is: [#126151]
13041
13042[#126151]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/126151
13043
13044------------------------
13045
13046When the `offset_of_slice` feature is enabled, the [`offset_of!`] macro may be used to determine
13047the offset of fields whose type is `[T]`, that is, a slice of dynamic size.
13048
13049In general, fields whose type is dynamically sized do not have statically known offsets because
13050they do not have statically known alignments. However, `[T]` has the same alignment as `T`, so
13051it specifically may be allowed.
13052
13053```rust
13054#![feature(offset_of_slice)]
13055
13056#[repr(C)]
13057pub struct Struct {
13058    head: u32,
13059    tail: [u8],
13060}
13061
13062fn main() {
13063    assert_eq!(std::mem::offset_of!(Struct, tail), 4);
13064}
13065```
13066
13067[`offset_of!`]: ../../std/mem/macro.offset_of.html

14482---
14483
14484This feature is incomplete and not yet intended for general use.
14485
14486This implements experimental, Edition-dependent match ergonomics under consideration for inclusion
14487in Rust, allowing `&` patterns in more places. For example:
14488
14489```rust,edition2024
14490#![feature(ref_pat_eat_one_layer_2024)]
14491#![allow(incomplete_features)]
14492#
14493# // Tests type equality in a way that avoids coercing `&&T` or `&mut T` to `&T`.
14494# trait Eq<T> {}
14495# impl<T> Eq<T> for T {}
14496# fn has_type<T>(_: impl Eq<T>) {}
14497
14498// `&` can match against a `ref` binding mode instead of a reference type:
14499let (x, &y) = &(0, 1);
14500has_type::<&u8>(x);
14501has_type::<u8>(y);
14502
14503// `&` can match against `&mut` references:
14504let &z = &mut 2;
14505has_type::<u8>(z);
14506```
14507
14508For specifics, see the corresponding typing rules for [Editions 2021 and earlier] and for
14509[Editions 2024 and later]. For more information on binding modes, see [The Rust Reference].
14510
14511For alternative experimental match ergonomics, see the feature
14512[`ref_pat_eat_one_layer_2024_structural`](./ref-pat-eat-one-layer-2024-structural.md).
14513
14514[Editions 2021 and earlier]: https://nadrieril.github.io/typing-rust-patterns/?compare=false&opts1=AQEBAQIBAQABAAAAAQEBAAEBAAABAAA%3D&mode=rules&do_cmp=false
14515[Editions 2024 and later]: https://nadrieril.github.io/typing-rust-patterns/?compare=false&opts1=AQEBAAABAQABAgIAAQEBAAEBAAABAAA%3D&mode=rules&do_cmp=false
14516[The Rust Reference]: https://doc.rust-lang.org/reference/patterns.html#binding-modes

14588
14589The tracking issue for this feature is: [#66079]
14590
14591[#66079]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/66079
14592
14593------------------------
14594
14595The `register_tool` language feature informs the compiler that attributes in your code are meant to be used with tools other than the compiler itself. This can be useful if your code has semantic meaning without the external tool, but enables additional features when the tool is present.
14596
14597`register_tool` also allows configuring lint levels for external tools.
14598
14599Tool attributes are only meant for ignorable attributes. If your code *changes* meaning when the attribute is present, it should not use a tool attribute (because it cannot be compiled with anything other than the external tool, and in a sense is a fork of the language).
14600
14601------------------------
14602
14603`#![register_tool(tool)]` is an attribute, and is only valid at the crate root.
14604Attributes using the registered tool are checked for valid syntax, and lint attributes are checked to be in a valid format. However, the compiler cannot validate the semantics of the attribute, nor can it tell whether the configured lint is present in the external tool.
14605
14606Semantically, `clippy::*`, `rustdoc::*`, and `rustfmt::*` lints and attributes all behave as if `#![register_tool(clippy, rustdoc, rustfmt)]` were injected into the crate root, except that the `rustdoc` namespace can only be used for lints, not for attributes.
14607When compiling with `-Z unstable-features`, `rustc::*` lints can also be used. Like `rustdoc`, the `rustc` namespace can only be used with lints, not attributes.
14608
14609The compiler will emit an error if it encounters a lint/attribute whose namespace isn't a registered tool.
14610
14611Tool namespaces cannot be nested; `register_tool(main_tool::subtool)` is an error.
14612
14613## Examples
14614
14615Tool attributes:
14616
14617```rust
14618#![feature(register_tool)]
14619#![register_tool(c2rust)]
14620
14621// Mark which C header file this module was generated from.
14622#[c2rust::header_src = "operations.h"]
14623pub mod operations_h {
14624    use std::ffi::c_int;
14625
14626    // Mark which source line this struct was generated from.
14627    #[c2rust::src_loc = "11:0"]
14628    pub struct Point {
14629        pub x: c_int,
14630        pub y: c_int,
14631    }
14632}
14633```
14634
14635Tool lints:
14636
14637```
14638#![feature(register_tool)]
14639#![register_tool(bevy)]
14640#![deny(bevy::duplicate_bevy_dependencies)]
14641```

14849    Lint {
14850        label: "rustc_attrs",
14851        description: r##"# `rustc_attrs`
14852
14853This feature has no tracking issue, and is therefore internal to
14854the compiler, not being intended for general use.
14855
14856Note: `rustc_attrs` enables many rustc-internal attributes and this page
14857only discuss a few of them.
14858
14859------------------------
14860
14861The `rustc_attrs` feature allows debugging rustc type layouts by using
14862`#[rustc_dump_layout(...)]` to debug layout at compile time (it even works
14863with `cargo check`) as an alternative to `rustc -Z print-type-sizes`
14864that is way more verbose.
14865
14866Options provided by `#[rustc_dump_layout(...)]` are `backend_repr`, `align`,
14867`debug`, `homogeneous_aggregate` and `size`.
14868Note that it only works on sized types without generics.
14869
14870## Examples
14871
14872```rust,compile_fail
14873#![feature(rustc_attrs)]
14874
14875#[rustc_dump_layout(backend_repr, size)]
14876pub enum X {
14877    Y(u8, u8, u8),
14878    Z(isize),
14879}
14880```
14881
14882When that is compiled, the compiler will error with something like
14883
14884```text
14885error: backend_repr: Aggregate { sized: true }
14886 --> src/lib.rs:4:1
14887  |
148884 | / pub enum T {
148895 | |     Y(u8, u8, u8),
148906 | |     Z(isize),
148917 | | }
14892  | |_^
14893
14894error: size: Size { raw: 16 }
14895 --> src/lib.rs:4:1
14896  |
148974 | / pub enum T {
148985 | |     Y(u8, u8, u8),
148996 | |     Z(isize),
149007 | | }
14901  | |_^
14902
14903error: aborting due to 2 previous errors
14904```

14911        label: "rustc_private",

14913
14914The tracking issue for this feature is: [#27812]
14915
14916[#27812]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/27812
14917
14918------------------------
14919
14920This feature allows access to unstable internal compiler crates such as `rustc_driver`.
14921
14922The presence of this feature changes the way the linkage format for dylibs is calculated in a way
14923that is necessary for linking against dylibs that statically link `std` (such as `rustc_driver`).
14924This makes this feature "viral" in linkage; its use in a given crate makes its use required in
14925dependent crates which link to it (including integration tests, which are built as separate crates).
14926
14927## Common linker failures related to missing LLVM libraries
14928
14929### When using `rustc-private` with Official Toolchains
14930
14931When using the `rustc_private` feature with official toolchains distributed via rustup, you'll need to install:
14932
149331. The `rustc-dev` component (provides compiler libraries)
149342. The `llvm-tools` component (provides LLVM libraries needed for linking)
14935
14936You can install these components using `rustup`:
14937
14938```text
14939rustup component add rustc-dev llvm-tools
14940```
14941
14942Without the `llvm-tools` component, you may encounter linking errors like:
14943
14944```text
14945error: linking with `cc` failed: exit status: 1
14946  |
14947  = note: rust-lld: error: unable to find library -lLLVM-{version}
14948```
14949
14950### When using `rustc-private` with Custom Toolchains
14951
14952For custom-built toolchains or environments not using rustup, different configuration may be required:
14953
14954- Ensure LLVM libraries are available in your library search paths
14955- You might need to configure library paths explicitly depending on your LLVM installation

15021        deny_since: None,
15022    },
15023    Lint {
15024        label: "sanitize",
15025        description: r##"# `sanitize`
15026
15027The tracking issue for this feature is: [#39699]
15028
15029[#39699]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/39699
15030
15031------------------------
15032
15033The `sanitize` attribute can be used to selectively disable or enable sanitizer
15034instrumentation in an annotated function. This might be useful to: avoid
15035instrumentation overhead in a performance critical function, or avoid
15036instrumenting code that contains constructs unsupported by given sanitizer.
15037
15038The precise effect of this annotation depends on particular sanitizer in use.
15039For example, with `sanitize(thread = "off")`, the thread sanitizer will no
15040longer instrument non-atomic store / load operations, but it will instrument
15041atomic operations to avoid reporting false positives and provide meaning full
15042stack traces.
15043
15044This attribute was previously named `no_sanitize`.
15045
15046## Examples
15047
15048``` rust
15049#![feature(sanitize)]
15050
15051#[sanitize(address = "off")]
15052fn foo() {
15053  // ...
15054}
15055```
15056
15057It is also possible to disable sanitizers for entire modules and enable them
15058for single items or functions.
15059
15060```rust
15061#![feature(sanitize)]
15062
15063#[sanitize(address = "off")]
15064mod foo {
15065  fn unsanitized() {
15066    // ...
15067  }
15068
15069  #[sanitize(address = "on")]
15070  fn sanitized() {
15071    // ...
15072  }
15073}
15074```
15075
15076It's also applicable to impl blocks.
15077
15078```rust
15079#![feature(sanitize)]
15080
15081trait MyTrait {
15082  fn foo(&self);
15083  fn bar(&self);
15084}
15085
15086#[sanitize(address = "off")]
15087impl MyTrait for () {
15088  fn foo(&self) {
15089    // ...
15090  }
15091
15092  #[sanitize(address = "on")]
15093  fn bar(&self) {
15094    // ...
15095  }
15096}
15097```

16011The tracking issue for this feature is: [#130351]
16012
16013[#130351]: https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/issues/130351
16014-----
16015
16016The `strict_provenance_lints` feature allows to enable the `implicit_provenance_casts` lint.
16017
16018## Example
16019
16020```rust
16021#![feature(strict_provenance_lints)]
16022#![warn(implicit_provenance_casts)]
16023
16024fn main() {
16025    let dangling = 16_usize as *const u8;
16026    //~^ WARNING: cast from `usize` to `*const u8` implicitly relies on exposed provenance
16027    let _addr = dangling as usize;
16028    //~^ WARNING: cast from `*const u8` to `usize` implicitly exposes pointer provenance
16029}
16030```

16242    Lint {
16243        label: "test",
16244        description: r##"# `test`
16245
16246The tracking issue for this feature is: None.
16247
16248------------------------
16249
16250The internals of the `test` crate are unstable, behind the `test` flag.  The
16251most widely used part of the `test` crate are benchmark tests, which can test
16252the performance of your code.  Let's make our `src/lib.rs` look like this
16253(comments elided):
16254
16255```rust,no_run
16256#![feature(test)]
16257
16258extern crate test;
16259
16260pub fn add_two(a: i32) -> i32 {
16261    a + 2
16262}
16263
16264#[cfg(test)]
16265mod tests {
16266    use super::*;
16267    use test::Bencher;
16268
16269    #[test]
16270    fn it_works() {
16271        assert_eq!(4, add_two(2));
16272    }
16273
16274    #[bench]
16275    fn bench_add_two(b: &mut Bencher) {
16276        b.iter(|| add_two(2));
16277    }
16278}
16279```
16280
16281Note the `test` feature gate, which enables this unstable feature.
16282
16283We've imported the `test` crate, which contains our benchmarking support.
16284We have a new function as well, with the `bench` attribute. Unlike regular
16285tests, which take no arguments, benchmark tests take a `&mut Bencher`. This
16286`Bencher` provides an `iter` method, which takes a closure. This closure
16287contains the code we'd like to benchmark.
16288
16289We can run benchmark tests with `cargo bench`:
16290
16291```bash
16292$ cargo bench
16293   Compiling adder v0.0.1 (file:///home/steve/tmp/adder)
16294     Running target/release/adder-91b3e234d4ed382a
16295
16296running 2 tests
16297test tests::it_works ... ignored
16298test tests::bench_add_two ... bench:         1 ns/iter (+/- 0)
16299
16300test result: ok. 0 passed; 0 failed; 1 ignored; 1 measured
16301```
16302
16303Our non-benchmark test was ignored. You may have noticed that `cargo bench`
16304takes a bit longer than `cargo test`. This is because Rust runs our benchmark
16305a number of times, and then takes the average. Because we're doing so little
16306work in this example, we have a `1 ns/iter (+/- 0)`, but this would show
16307the variance if there was one.
16308
16309Advice on writing benchmarks:
16310
16311
16312* Move setup code outside the `iter` loop; only put the part you want to measure inside
16313* Make the code do "the same thing" on each iteration; do not accumulate or change state
16314* Make the outer function idempotent too; the benchmark runner is likely to run
16315  it many times
16316*  Make the inner `iter` loop short and fast so benchmark runs are fast and the
16317   calibrator can adjust the run-length at fine resolution
16318* Make the code in the `iter` loop do something simple, to assist in pinpointing
16319  performance improvements (or regressions)
16320
16321## Gotcha: optimizations
16322
16323There's another tricky part to writing benchmarks: benchmarks compiled with
16324optimizations activated can be dramatically changed by the optimizer so that
16325the benchmark is no longer benchmarking what one expects. For example, the
16326compiler might recognize that some calculation has no external effects and
16327remove it entirely.
16328
16329```rust,no_run
16330#![feature(test)]
16331
16332extern crate test;
16333use test::Bencher;
16334
16335#[bench]
16336fn bench_xor_1000_ints(b: &mut Bencher) {
16337    b.iter(|| {
16338        (0..1000).fold(0, |old, new| old ^ new);
16339    });
16340}
16341```
16342
16343gives the following results
16344
16345```text
16346running 1 test
16347test bench_xor_1000_ints ... bench:         0 ns/iter (+/- 0)
16348
16349test result: ok. 0 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 1 measured
16350```
16351
16352The benchmarking runner offers two ways to avoid this. Either, the closure that
16353the `iter` method receives can return an arbitrary value which forces the
16354optimizer to consider the result used and ensures it cannot remove the
16355computation entirely. This could be done for the example above by adjusting the
16356`b.iter` call to
16357
16358```rust
16359# struct X;
16360# impl X { fn iter<T, F>(&self, _: F) where F: FnMut() -> T {} } let b = X;
16361b.iter(|| {
16362    // Note lack of `;` (could also use an explicit `return`).
16363    (0..1000).fold(0, |old, new| old ^ new)
16364});
16365```
16366
16367Or, the other option is to call the generic `test::black_box` function, which
16368is an opaque "black box" to the optimizer and so forces it to consider any
16369argument as used.
16370
16371```rust
16372#![feature(test)]
16373
16374extern crate test;
16375
16376# fn main() {
16377# struct X;
16378# impl X { fn iter<T, F>(&self, _: F) where F: FnMut() -> T {} } let b = X;
16379b.iter(|| {
16380    let n = test::black_box(1000);
16381
16382    (0..n).fold(0, |a, b| a ^ b)
16383})
16384# }
16385```
16386
16387Neither of these read or modify the value, and are very cheap for small values.
16388Larger values can be passed indirectly to reduce overhead (e.g.
16389`black_box(&huge_struct)`).
16390
16391Performing either of the above changes gives the following benchmarking results
16392
16393```text
16394running 1 test
16395test bench_xor_1000_ints ... bench:       131 ns/iter (+/- 3)
16396
16397test result: ok. 0 passed; 0 failed; 0 ignored; 1 measured
16398```
16399
16400However, the optimizer can still modify a testcase in an undesirable manner
16401even when using either of the above.

16630
16631With `trace_macros` you can trace the expansion of macros in your code.
16632
16633## Examples
16634
16635```rust
16636#![feature(trace_macros)]
16637
16638fn main() {
16639    trace_macros!(true);
16640    println!("Hello, Rust!");
16641    trace_macros!(false);
16642}
16643```
16644
16645The `cargo build` output:
16646
16647```txt
16648note: trace_macro
16649 --> src/main.rs:5:5
16650  |
166515 |     println!("Hello, Rust!");
16652  |     ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
16653  |
16654  = note: expanding `println! { "Hello, Rust!" }`
16655  = note: to `print ! ( concat ! ( "Hello, Rust!" , "\n" ) )`
16656  = note: expanding `print! { concat ! ( "Hello, Rust!" , "\n" ) }`
16657  = note: to `$crate :: io :: _print ( format_args ! ( concat ! ( "Hello, Rust!" , "\n" ) )
16658          )`
16659
16660    Finished dev [unoptimized + debuginfo] target(s) in 0.60 secs
16661```

16676
16677The `trait_alias` feature adds support for trait aliases. These allow aliases
16678to be created for one or more traits (currently just a single regular trait plus
16679any number of auto-traits), and used wherever traits would normally be used as
16680either bounds or trait objects.
16681
16682```rust
16683#![feature(trait_alias)]
16684
16685trait Foo = std::fmt::Debug + Send;
16686trait Bar = Foo + Sync;
16687
16688// Use trait alias as bound on type parameter.
16689fn foo<T: Foo>(v: &T) {
16690    println!("{:?}", v);
16691}
16692
16693pub fn main() {
16694    foo(&1);
16695
16696    // Use trait alias for trait objects.
16697    let a: &dyn Bar = &123;
16698    println!("{:?}", a);
16699    let b = Box::new(456) as Box<dyn Foo>;
16700    println!("{:?}", b);
16701}
16702```

16780----
16781
16782The `transparent_unions` feature allows you mark `union`s as
16783`#[repr(transparent)]`. A `union` may be `#[repr(transparent)]` in exactly the
16784same conditions in which a `struct` may be `#[repr(transparent)]` (generally,
16785this means the `union` must have exactly one non-zero-sized field). Some
16786concrete illustrations follow.
16787
16788```rust
16789#![feature(transparent_unions)]
16790
16791// This union has the same representation as `f32`.
16792#[repr(transparent)]
16793union SingleFieldUnion {
16794    field: f32,
16795}
16796
16797// This union has the same representation as `usize`.
16798#[repr(transparent)]
16799union MultiFieldUnion {
16800    field: usize,
16801    nothing: (),
16802}
16803```
16804
16805For consistency with transparent `struct`s, `union`s must have exactly one
16806non-zero-sized field. If all fields are zero-sized, the `union` must not be
16807`#[repr(transparent)]`:
16808
16809```rust
16810#![feature(transparent_unions)]
16811
16812// This (non-transparent) union is already valid in stable Rust:
16813pub union GoodUnion {
16814    pub nothing: (),
16815}
16816
16817// Error: transparent union needs exactly one non-zero-sized field, but has 0
16818// #[repr(transparent)]
16819// pub union BadUnion {
16820//     pub nothing: (),
16821// }
16822```
16823
16824The one exception is if the `union` is generic over `T` and has a field of type
16825`T`, it may be `#[repr(transparent)]` even if `T` is a zero-sized type:
16826
16827```rust
16828#![feature(transparent_unions)]
16829
16830// This union has the same representation as `T`.
16831#[repr(transparent)]
16832pub union GenericUnion<T: Copy> { // Unions with non-`Copy` fields are unstable.
16833    pub field: T,
16834    pub nothing: (),
16835}
16836
16837// This is okay even though `()` is a zero-sized type.
16838pub const THIS_IS_OKAY: GenericUnion<()> = GenericUnion { field: () };
16839```
16840
16841Like transparent `struct`s, a transparent `union` of type `U` has the same
16842layout, size, and ABI as its single non-ZST field. If it is generic over a type
16843`T`, and all its fields are ZSTs except for exactly one field of type `T`, then
16844it has the same layout and ABI as `T` (even if `T` is a ZST when monomorphized).
16845
16846Like transparent `struct`s, transparent `union`s are FFI-safe if and only if
16847their underlying representation type is also FFI-safe.
16848
16849A `union` may not be eligible for the same nonnull-style optimizations that a
16850`struct` or `enum` (with the same fields) are eligible for. Adding
16851`#[repr(transparent)]` to  `union` does not change this. To give a more concrete
16852example, it is unspecified whether `size_of::<T>()` is equal to
16853`size_of::<Option<T>>()`, where `T` is a `union` (regardless of whether or not
16854it is transparent). The Rust compiler is free to perform this optimization if
16855possible, but is not required to, and different compiler versions may differ in
16856their application of these optimizations.

16960------------------------
16961
16962The `try_as_dyn` feature allows going from a generic `T` with no bounds
16963to a `dyn Trait`, if `T: Trait` and various conditions are upheld. It is
16964very related to specialization, as it allows you to specialize within
16965function bodies, but in a more general manner than `Any::downcast`.
16966
16967```rust
16968#![feature(try_as_dyn)]
16969
16970fn downcast_debug_format<T: 'static>(t: &T) -> String {
16971    match std::any::try_as_dyn::<_, dyn std::fmt::Debug>(t) {
16972        Some(d) => format!("{d:?}"),
16973        None => "default".to_string()
16974    }
16975}
16976```
16977
16978
16979## Rules and reasons for them
16980
16981> [!IMPORTANT]
16982> The main problem of **`try_as_dyn` and specialization is the compiler's inability, while trait-checking, to distinguish/_discriminate_ between any two given lifetimes**[^1].
16983
16984[^1]: the compiler cannot _branch_ on whether "`'a : 'b` holds": for soundness, it can either choose not to know the answer, or _assume_ that it holds and produce an obligation for the borrow-checker which shall "assert this" (making compilation fail in a fatal manner if not). Most usages of Rust lie in the latter category (typical `where` clauses anywhere), whilst specialization/`try_as_dyn()` wants to support fallibility of the operation (_i.e._, being queried on a type not fulfilling the predicate without causing a compilation error). This rules out the latter, resulting in the need for the former, _i.e._, for the `try_as_dyn()` attempt to unconditionally "fail" with `None`.
16985
16986### `'static` is not mentioned anywhere in the `impl` block header.
16987
16988The most obvious one: if you have `impl IsStatic for &'static str`, then determining whether `&'? str : IsStatic` does hold amounts to discriminating `'? : 'static`.
16989
16990### Each outlives `where` bound (`Type: 'a` and `'a: 'b`) does not mention lifetime-infected parameters.
16991
16992Parameters are considered lifetime-infected if they are defined in an `impl` block's generic parameter list.
16993Const generics are exempt, as they can't affect lifetimes.
16994`for<'a>` lifetimes (and in the future types) are not lifetime-infected.
16995
16996We can create lifetime discrimination this way. For instance, given `impl<'a, 'b> Outlives<'a> for &'b str where 'b : 'a {}`, `Outlives<'static>` amounts to `IsStatic` from previous bullet.
16997
16998### Each lifetime-infected parameter is mentioned at most once in the `Self` type and the implemented trait's generic parameters, combined.
16999
17000Repetition of a parameter entails equality of those two use-sites; in lifetime-terms, this would be a double `'a : 'b` / `'b : 'a` clause, for instance.
17001Follow-up from the previous example: `impl<'a> Uses<'a> for &'a str {}`, and check whether `&'? str : Uses<'static>`.
17002
17003### Each individual trait where bound (`Type: Trait`) mentions each lifetime-infected parameter at most once.
17004
17005Mentioning a lifetime-infected parameter in multiple `where` bounds is allowed.
17006
17007Looking at the previous rules, which focuses on `Self : …`, this is just observing that shifting the requirements to other parameters within `where` clauses \[ought to\] boil down to the same set of issues.
17008
17009This is _unnecessarily restrictive_: we should be able to loosen it up somehow. Repetition only in `where` clauses seems fine.
17010
17011
17012### The `impl` block is a handwritten impl
17013
17014as opposed to a type implementing a trait automatically by the compiler (such as auto-traits, `dyn Bounds… : Bounds…`, and closures)
17015
17016
17017The reason for this is that some such auto-generated impls _come with hidden bounds or whatnot_, which run afoul of the previous rules, whilst also being _extremely challenging for the current compiler logic to know of such bounds_.
17018IIUC, this restriction could be lifted in the future should the compiler logic be better at spotting these hidden bounds, when present.
17019
17020One contrived such example being the case of `dyn 'u + for<'a> Outlives<'a>`, where the compiler-generated `impl` for it of `Outlives` is: `impl<'b, 'u> Outlives<'b> for dyn 'u + for<'a> Outlives<'a> where 'b : 'u {}` which violates the "`'a: 'b` not to mention lt-infected params" rule, whilst also being hard to detect in current compiler logic.
17021
17022### Associated type projections (`<Type as Trait>::Assoc`) are not mentioned anywhere in the `impl` block header.
17023
17024Associated-type equality bounds can very much amount to lifetime-infected parameter equality constraints,
17025which are problematic as per the "at most one mention of each lifetime-infected parameter in header" rule.
17026To illustrate, with the following definitions, `&'? str: Trait<'static>` discriminates `'?` against `'static`:
17027```rust
17028trait Trait<'x> {}
17029impl<'a, 'b> Trait<'b> for &'a str
17030where
17031    //     &'a str = &'b str,
17032    Option<&'a str>: IntoIterator<Item = &'b str>,
17033{}
17034```
17035
17036```rust
17037trait Trait<'x> {}
17038impl<'a> Trait<'a> for &'a str {}
17039```
17040
17041### Each trait `where` bound with an associated type equality (`Type: Trait<Assoc = Type2>`) does not mention lifetime-infected parameters.
17042
17043Checking whether `Option<&'? str>: IntoIterator<Item = &'static str>` holds discriminates `'?` against `'static`.

17058
17059The `try_blocks` feature adds support for `try` blocks. A `try`
17060block creates a new scope one can use the `?` operator in.
17061
17062```rust,edition2018
17063#![feature(try_blocks)]
17064
17065use std::num::ParseIntError;
17066
17067let result = try {
17068    "1".parse::<i32>()?
17069        + "2".parse::<i32>()?
17070        + "3".parse::<i32>()?
17071};
17072assert_eq!(result, Ok(6));
17073
17074let result = try {
17075    "1".parse::<i32>()?
17076        + "foo".parse::<i32>()?
17077        + "3".parse::<i32>()?
17078};
17079assert!(result.is_err());
17080```

17265
17266> This feature is not to be confused with [`trait_alias`] or [`impl_trait_in_assoc_type`].
17267
17268### What is `impl Trait`?
17269
17270`impl Trait` in return position is useful for declaring types that are constrained by traits, but whose concrete type should be hidden:
17271
17272```rust
17273use std::fmt::Debug;
17274
17275fn new() -> impl Debug {
17276    42
17277}
17278
17279fn main() {
17280    let thing = new();
17281    // What actually is a `thing`?
17282    // No idea but we know it implements `Debug`, so we can debug print it
17283    println!("{thing:?}");
17284}
17285```
17286
17287See the [reference] for more information about `impl Trait` in return position.
17288
17289### `type_alias_impl_trait`
17290
17291However, we might want to use an `impl Trait` in multiple locations but actually use the same concrete type everywhere while keeping it hidden.
17292This can be useful in libraries where you want to hide implementation details.
17293
17294The `#[define_opaque]` attribute must be used to explicitly list opaque items constrained by the item it's on.
17295
17296```rust
17297#![feature(type_alias_impl_trait)]
17298# #![allow(unused_variables, dead_code)]
17299trait Trait {}
17300
17301struct MyType;
17302
17303impl Trait for MyType {}
17304
17305type Alias = impl Trait;
17306
17307#[define_opaque(Alias)] // To constrain the type alias to `MyType`
17308fn new() -> Alias {
17309    MyType
17310}
17311
17312#[define_opaque(Alias)] // So we can name the concrete type inside this item
17313fn main() {
17314    let thing: MyType = new();
17315}
17316
17317// It can be a part of a struct too
17318struct HaveAlias {
17319    stuff: String,
17320    thing: Alias,
17321}
17322```
17323
17324In this example, the concrete type referred to by `Alias` is guaranteed to be the same wherever `Alias` occurs.
17325
17326> Originally this feature included type aliases as an associated type of a trait. In [#110237] this was split off to [`impl_trait_in_assoc_type`].
17327
17328### `type_alias_impl_trait` in argument position.
17329
17330Note that using `Alias` as an argument type is *not* the same as argument-position `impl Trait`, as `Alias` refers to a unique type, whereas the concrete type for argument-position `impl Trait` is chosen by the caller.
17331
17332```rust
17333# #![feature(type_alias_impl_trait)]
17334# #![allow(unused_variables)]
17335# pub mod x {
17336# pub trait Trait {}
17337#
17338# struct MyType;
17339#
17340# impl Trait for MyType {}
17341#
17342# pub type Alias = impl Trait;
17343#
17344# #[define_opaque(Alias)]
17345# pub fn new() -> Alias {
17346#     MyType
17347# }
17348# }
17349# use x::*;
17350// this...
17351pub fn take_alias(x: Alias) {
17352    // ...
17353}
17354
17355// ...is *not* the same as
17356pub fn take_impl(x: impl Trait) {
17357    // ...
17358}
17359# fn main(){}
17360```
17361
17362```rust,compile_fail,E0308
17363# #![feature(type_alias_impl_trait)]
17364# #![allow(unused_variables)]
17365# pub mod x {
17366# pub trait Trait {}
17367#
17368# struct MyType;
17369#
17370# impl Trait for MyType {}
17371#
17372# pub type Alias = impl Trait;
17373#
17374# #[define_opaque(Alias)]
17375# pub fn new() -> Alias {
17376#     MyType
17377# }
17378# }
17379# use x::*;
17380# pub fn take_alias(x: Alias) {
17381#     // ...
17382# }
17383#
17384# pub fn take_impl(x: impl Trait) {
17385#    // ...
17386# }
17387#
17388// a user's crate using the trait and type alias
17389struct UserType;
17390impl Trait for UserType {}
17391
17392# fn main(){
17393let x = UserType;
17394take_alias(x);
17395// ERROR expected opaque type, found `UserType`
17396// this function *actually* takes a `MyType` as is constrained in `new`
17397
17398let x = UserType;
17399take_impl(x);
17400// OK
17401
17402let x = new();
17403take_alias(x);
17404// OK
17405
17406let x = new();
17407take_impl(x);
17408// OK
17409# }
17410```
17411
17412Note that the user cannot use `#[define_opaque(Alias)]` to reify the opaque type because only the crate where the type alias is declared may do so. But if this happened in the same crate and the opaque type was reified, they'd get a familiar error: "expected `MyType`, got `UserType`".

17449
17450This implements [RFC2528]. When turned on, you can create instances of the same struct
17451that have different generic type or lifetime parameters.
17452
17453[RFC2528]: https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/2528-type-changing-struct-update-syntax.html
17454
17455```rust
17456#![allow(unused_variables, dead_code)]
17457#![feature(type_changing_struct_update)]
17458
17459fn main () {
17460    struct Foo<T, U> {
17461        field1: T,
17462        field2: U,
17463    }
17464
17465    let base: Foo<String, i32> = Foo {
17466        field1: String::from("hello"),
17467        field2: 1234,
17468    };
17469    let updated: Foo<f64, i32> = Foo {
17470        field1: 3.14,
17471        ..base
17472    };
17473}

17584----
17585
17586The `unboxed_closures` feature allows you to write functions using the `"rust-call"` ABI,
17587required for implementing the [`Fn*`] family of traits. `"rust-call"` functions must have
17588exactly one (non self) argument, a tuple representing the argument list.
17589
17590[`Fn*`]: ../../std/ops/trait.Fn.html
17591
17592```rust
17593#![feature(unboxed_closures)]
17594
17595extern "rust-call" fn add_args(args: (u32, u32)) -> u32 {
17596    args.0 + args.1
17597}
17598
17599fn main() {}
17600```

18642The `yeet_expr` feature adds support for `do yeet` expressions,
18643which can be used to early-exit from a function or `try` block.
18644
18645These are highly experimental, thus the placeholder syntax.
18646
18647```rust,edition2021
18648#![feature(yeet_expr)]
18649
18650fn foo() -> Result<String, i32> {
18651    do yeet 4;
18652}
18653assert_eq!(foo(), Err(4));
18654
18655fn bar() -> Option<String> {
18656    do yeet;
18657}
18658assert_eq!(bar(), None);
18659```

18871    Lint {
18872        label: "clippy::bad_bit_mask",
18873        description: r##"Checks for incompatible bit masks in comparisons.
18874
18875The formula for detecting if an expression of the type `_ <bit_op> m
18876<cmp_op> c` (where `<bit_op>` is one of {`&`, `|`} and `<cmp_op>` is one of
18877{`!=`, `>=`, `>`, `!=`, `>=`, `>`}) can be determined from the following
18878table:
18879
18880|Comparison  |Bit Op|Example      |is always|Formula               |
18881|------------|------|-------------|---------|----------------------|
18882|`==` or `!=`| `&`  |`x & 2 == 3` |`false`  |`c & m != c`          |
18883|`<`  or `>=`| `&`  |`x & 2 < 3`  |`true`   |`m < c`               |
18884|`>`  or `<=`| `&`  |`x & 1 > 1`  |`false`  |`m <= c`              |
18885|`==` or `!=`| `\\|` |`x \\| 1 == 0`|`false`  |`c \\| m != c`         |
18886|`<`  or `>=`| `\\|` |`x \\| 1 < 1` |`false`  |`m >= c`              |
18887|`<=` or `>` | `\\|` |`x \\| 1 > 0` |`true`   |`m > c`               |"##,
18888        default_severity: Severity::Allow,
18889        warn_since: None,
18890        deny_since: None,
18891    },

22448against or the pattern itself, as well as the bindings that are introduced by the

24639        description: r##"Checks for methods with certain name prefixes or suffixes, and which
24640do not adhere to standard conventions regarding how `self` is taken.
24641The actual rules are:
24642
24643|Prefix |Postfix     |`self` taken                   | `self` type  |
24644|-------|------------|-------------------------------|--------------|
24645|`as_`  | none       |`&self` or `&mut self`         | any          |
24646|`from_`| none       | none                          | any          |
24647|`into_`| none       |`self`                         | any          |
24648|`is_`  | none       |`&mut self` or `&self` or none | any          |
24649|`to_`  | `_mut`     |`&mut self`                    | any          |
24650|`to_`  | not `_mut` |`self`                         | `Copy`       |
24651|`to_`  | not `_mut` |`&self`                        | not `Copy`   |
24652
24653Note: Clippy doesn't trigger methods with `to_` prefix in:
24654- Traits definition.
24655Clippy can not tell if a type that implements a trait is `Copy` or not.
24656- Traits implementation, when `&self` is taken.
24657The method signature is controlled by the trait and often `&self` is required for all types that implement the trait
24658(see e.g. the `std::string::ToString` trait).
24659
24660Clippy allows `Pin<&Self>` and `Pin<&mut Self>` if `&self` and `&mut self` is required.
24661
24662Please find more info here:
24663https://rust-lang.github.io/api-guidelines/naming.html#ad-hoc-conversions-follow-as_-to_-into_-conventions-c-conv"##,
